weeks.title: Sunday: The Worship of Offering Ourselves
weeks.keyText: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.
weeks.theme: Sunday is not about going to watch a service; it is about laying myself on the altar.
group: Read Romans 12:1. What might it look like to “present your bodies a living sacrifice” in a Sunday service?
Have you ever judged a Sunday service by whether it was “good to watch” or “good to listen to”? What does that reveal?
As a small group, agree on one way to prepare for Sunday (such as arriving early or praying for the preacher). How will you remind one another this week?
weeks.sunday: Go to bed a little earlier the night before, and pray for the preacher, the pianist, and any newcomers. As you walk into the sanctuary, pray silently, “Lord, I’ve come to offer myself.” When you sing, pay attention to the words and sing to the Lord from your heart; as you listen to the sermon, write down one sentence you will put into practice. Before you leave, go and greet someone you don’t know.

lessons.title: A Living Sacrifice on the Altar
lessons.hear:
The word “sacrifice” feels a little foreign to us today. In the Old Testament, worship was inseparable from the altar: cattle and sheep were led before it, slaughtered, and burned, given wholly to God. So when Paul wrote, “present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God” (Romans 12:1), the first believers understood immediately. Worship is not spectating; it is offering. And it is not offering God a little something of mine; it is offering myself.

But Paul added a startling adjective: a “living” sacrifice. In the Old Testament, the offering died the moment it was placed on the altar. The New Testament offering is presented alive—and must be presented again every day. The great difficulty with a living sacrifice is that it keeps crawling off the altar. We offer ourselves on Sunday morning, and by the time we are fighting for a spot in the parking lot, we have often climbed right back down.

Notice the ground of it all: “I urge you … by the mercies of God.” Worship does not begin with our zeal; it begins with God’s mercy. The first eleven chapters of Romans describe how God has poured out grace on sinners in Christ, and worship is the most natural response of a heart moved by that grace. The psalmist issues the same invitation: “Oh come, let’s worship and bow down. Let’s kneel before the LORD, our Maker” (Psalm 95:6). To bow down is to confess that he is God and I am not.

So Sunday is not a weekly religious program. It is a gathering of living sacrifices who say to God together, “I am yours.” Singing, prayer, preaching, giving, the breaking of bread—the order of service differs from one tradition to another, but the heart of it is the same: offering ourselves. Jesus said the Father seeks those who “worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23). He wants more than my attendance; he wants my heart.

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you: Do I come before God with my whole self? Or do I bring only my body to the pew while my heart stays somewhere else?
lessons.light: Self-centered worship asks, “What do I get out of it?” Selfless worship asks, “What does the Lord receive?” To let Jesus reign is to hold nothing back on the altar—our time, our preferences, our pride, and our plans all go on it. Change your mindset and you change your life: when Sunday shifts from “watching a service” to “offering myself,” the whole week begins to become worship.
think: In Romans 12:1, what does Paul use as the basis for his appeal?
When was the last Sunday I truly “offered myself”?
Which part of me is most tempted to “crawl off the altar” this week?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that your mercy reached me first. I confess that I often bring my body to church while my heart stays elsewhere. Today I offer myself to you again: my time, my preferences, and my plans all belong to you. Holy Spirit, make me a living sacrifice, not only on Sunday but every day. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight before bed, take three minutes to write down the one thing you most want to keep for yourself this week, and pray as you hand it to the Lord. This Sunday, as you walk into the sanctuary (or open the livestream), quietly offer it to him again.
lessons.quick: Worship is not watching a service; it is laying myself on the altar.
text: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.
Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.

lessons.title: Audience, Actors, and the One
lessons.hear:
Every Sunday on the drive home, one sister used to “rate” the service. The songs were too slow today—three stars. The sermon ran a bit long, but the illustrations were good—four stars. Then one day her daughter, who was in elementary school, asked, “Mom, what did Jesus think of our singing today?” She had no answer.

Our old mindset often treats Sunday as a performance: the people on stage are the actors, the people in the seats are the audience, and whether the service was good depends on how the stage performed. The nineteenth-century Danish thinker Søren Kierkegaard once offered a picture that went something like this: in true worship, the congregation are the actors, the leaders are only prompters standing in the wings, and the audience is just One—God himself.

The Samaritan woman came to Jesus with an old mindset too. Should we worship on this mountain, or in Jerusalem? She was concerned with place and form. Jesus turned her question from “where” to “how”: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). In spirit means from the inside, by the Holy Spirit; in truth means according to the truth, without pretense.

This does not mean the songs and the sermon don’t matter; faithful leaders should prepare with all their heart. It means that whether worship succeeds is not decided on the stage but in every heart. In the Old Testament, God rebuked his people for offering blind and lame animals: “Present it now to your governor! Will he be pleased with you? Or will he accept your person?” (Malachi 1:8). We prepare early and dress carefully for a job interview, yet we often arrive late, empty-hearted, and scrolling on our phones when we come before the King of kings.

That sister eventually changed a habit. On the drive home, she no longer handed out ratings. Instead, the family took turns answering two questions: “What did I offer today? What did I receive from the Lord today?” The atmosphere in the car changed—and so did her heart.
lessons.light: A consumer mindset puts us in the judge’s seat, and that is leaving our proper place—we are worshipers, not judges. Humility means returning to our proper place: letting God be God and letting me be the one who bows. When our focus shifts from the stage back to the throne, and from others back to our own hearts, Sunday becomes a meeting with the Lord once more.
think: How did Jesus turn the woman’s question from “place” to “heart”?
Do I often judge a service by the performance on stage?
Next Sunday, what offering “without blemish” will I bring?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, forgive me for so often sitting in the judge’s seat—critiquing the songs and grading the sermon—and forgetting that you are the One. Help me worship you in spirit and truth, and bless the brothers and sisters who serve up front and behind the scenes. Keep my focus on you during the service. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, send a thank-you message to someone who serves on Sundays (the pianist, the sound tech, a greeter, or the preacher), and tell them specifically how their service helped you worship.
lessons.quick: Sunday has an audience of One; I am a worshiper, not a judge.
text: The woman said to him, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.
Our fathers worshiped in this mountain, and you Jews say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”
Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither in this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.
You worship that which you don’t know. We worship that which we know; for salvation is from the Jews.
But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.
God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”

lessons.title: Sunday Starts the Night Before
lessons.hear:
Athletes warm up before a game. Musicians tune up before they go on stage. Worship needs preparation too. Many of us roll out of bed on Sunday morning in a rush, argue in the car, arrive ten minutes late, and sit down with our hearts still out of breath—then conclude, “I didn’t feel anything in church today.” It isn’t that God was absent from the service; it’s that we never prepared our hearts.

Psalm 95 is like a map of worship. First comes joyful shouting: “Oh come, let’s sing to the LORD. Let’s shout aloud to the rock of our salvation!” (Psalm 95:1). Then come bowing and kneeling. Finally comes listening: “Today, oh that you would hear his voice!” (Psalm 95:7). From thanksgiving to surrender, and from surrender to listening—this is the very rhythm of a Sunday service.

You can begin practicing three small things today. First, prepare the night before: go to bed early, set out your Bible and your offering, and pray for the preacher, the worship leaders, and any newcomers. Second, arrive ten minutes early—not to grab a good seat, but to be still and to greet people. Thank the greeters, and nod and smile at the new face sitting in the corner. Third, listen with expectation: open your notebook, ask the Lord for one word, and before you get home, share that word with someone.

If you join online, the same applies: close your other windows, sit up, sing along, and don’t let the service become background music.

The psalmist says, “For a day in your courts is better than a thousand. I” (Psalm 84:10). When we prepare our hearts, Sunday is no longer the week’s obligation but the week’s high point. Better still, your preparation blesses others: one person worshiping wholeheartedly makes it easier for the whole row to focus.
lessons.light: Use your heart and rely on the Holy Spirit; don’t use only your head and rely on yourself. Preparing for Sunday is not one more chore; it brings the heart back into focus—focused on Jesus, not on the crowded parking lot or last night’s argument. In our relationships, God comes first; when I am first aligned with God, I can see the people around me in the service far more clearly.
think: In Psalm 95:1-7, what are the different actions of worship?
In what state do I usually arrive at church on Sunday morning?
This Saturday night, what one thing will I do to prepare for Sunday?
lessons.speak: Father, I so often bring you my most tired and hurried self. This week, help me prepare well: to grow quiet early, to pray for those who serve, and to come expecting to hear your word. Make me a blessing to others in the service, so that newcomers can feel the warmth of your family. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: On Saturday night, pray for one minute each for this Sunday’s preacher and for a newcomer (or a member you haven’t seen in a while). On Sunday, arrive ten minutes early and go greet that newcomer.
lessons.quick: Prepare your heart, and Sunday turns from an obligation into the high point of the week.
text: Oh come, let’s sing to the LORD. Let’s shout aloud to the rock of our salvation!
Let’s come before his presence with thanksgiving. Let’s extol him with songs!
For the LORD is a great God, a great King above all gods.
In his hand are the deep places of the earth. The heights of the mountains are also his.
The sea is his, and he made it. His hands formed the dry land.
Oh come, let’s worship and bow down. Let’s kneel before the LORD, our Maker,
for he is our God. We are the people of his pasture, and the sheep in his care. Today, oh that you would hear his voice!

lessons.title: Woe Is Me! I Am Undone
lessons.hear:
Isaiah knew every ritual of the temple, and he was an outstanding prophet. Yet in the year King Uzziah died, he saw in the temple something he had never seen before: “I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1). The seraphim covered their faces and called to one another, “Holy, holy, holy,” and even the foundations of the thresholds shook.

In that moment Isaiah did not say, “What wonderful worship today!” He said, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). The first response to truly seeing God is not a good feeling; it is seeing yourself. And notice what he confessed: the very thing a prophet relies on most—his lips.

Today, examine yourself before the Lord: Where is self at the center of my worship? Perhaps when I sing, I care about whether my voice sounds good. Perhaps on the choir or worship team, I care about who stands in the middle and who holds the microphone. Perhaps during the sermon I keep thinking, “So-and-so really needs to hear this.” Perhaps I treat giving as a transaction, hoping to get a blessing in return. All of these put me on the throne instead of the Lord.

But Isaiah’s story does not stop at “woe is me.” A seraph took a live coal from the altar and touched his mouth: “Your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven” (Isaiah 6:7). The end of self-examination is not condemnation but cleansing. That coal from the altar reminds us of the complete forgiveness won on the cross.

Once he was forgiven, Isaiah heard the Lord say, “Whom shall I send?” And he answered, “Here I am. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8). This is the direction of our adjustment: from “I want to be moved” back to “Lord, here I am.” Worship is not complete when the service ends; it is complete when I am sent out.
lessons.light: Pride can put on spiritual clothing even in worship: wanting to be seen, wanting to be praised, wanting to be the star. Humility means returning to our proper place: before the throne, I am simply someone who needs to be cleansed by the coal. Selfless worshipers don’t compare and don’t perform; they simply say, “Lord, here I am.”
think: After Isaiah saw the Lord, what changes did he go through?
In worship or ministry, what do I most want others to notice about me?
This Sunday, how will I say to the Lord, “Here I am”?
lessons.speak: Holy Lord, when I see your glory, I also see my own uncleanness. Forgive me for still wanting to be the star and to be seen, even in worship. Cleanse my lips and my heart with the forgiveness of the cross, so that I no longer sing for myself or serve for myself. Lord, here I am. Send me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Take ten quiet minutes today to read Isaiah 6:1-8. Write down one way you have been self-centered in worship and confess it to the Lord. If this has led you to compare yourself with a ministry team member or to hold something against them, pray a blessing over that person today.
lessons.quick: To see God is to see yourself; the cleansed say, “Here I am.”
text: In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple.
Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew.
One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”
The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.
Then I said, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips and I live among a people of unclean lips, for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Armies!”
Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar.
He touched my mouth with it, and said, “Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven.”
I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am. Send me!”

lessons.title: Taking Worship Beyond the Sanctuary
lessons.hear:
This week we have taken a fresh look at Sunday: worship is offering ourselves, coming before God in spirit and truth, preparing our hearts, humbling ourselves before the throne, and then being sent out. Now let’s carry what we have received beyond the sanctuary and pass it on to others.

Paul gave the Colossian church a picture of their gatherings: “teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord” (Colossians 3:16). Notice the words “one another.” Worship is not only the vertical relationship between me and God; it also flows horizontally among the members of the body. The song you sing may become encouragement for the weary brother beside you; one sentence you share from what you received may be exactly the word a sister needs this week.

Then Paul says, “Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus” (Colossians 3:17). Sunday is the gathering point of worship, but it is not the end point. Monday’s meeting, Tuesday’s kitchen, and Wednesday’s classroom are all places where the living sacrifice keeps being offered. Sunday gathers us; the weekdays scatter us. We gather to be filled, and we scatter to bless.

God’s people in the Old Testament were commanded to teach his words diligently to their children, talking of them when they sat at home and when they walked along the road (see Deuteronomy 6:7). Multiplication today can be just as simple: tell one person what you have newly understood about worship this week. Maybe you tell your child, “We don’t go to church on Sunday to watch a show; we go to give ourselves to God.” Maybe you invite a friend who hasn’t come in a long time: “Want to come with me this Sunday? I’ll wait for you at the door.”

One worshiper who wakes up can wake up a whole row; a whole row of awakened worshipers can change the atmosphere of an entire church.
lessons.light: The last step of changing a mindset is multiplication. If worship stays only in my heart, it remains a private feeling; when it flows out, it becomes the life of the body. Start with the “2” beside you—passing on the conviction that “Sunday is about offering myself” to one person is how we build God’s system on earth.
think: In Colossians 3:16-17, how are our gatherings connected with everyday life?
What has concretely changed in the way I see Sunday this week?
Whom will I invite to join me this Sunday?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for renewing the way I see worship this week. May my Sundays be an offering, and may my weekdays carry that worship forward. Use one sentence or one invitation from me to wake up the people around me to worship you together, so that you receive all the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, message a friend or church member who hasn’t been to church in a long time and invite them to worship with you this Sunday. Arrange to wait for them at the door (or online).
lessons.quick: Sunday gathers us and the weekdays scatter us; every place becomes an altar.
text: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.
Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

weeks.title: Don’t Stop Meeting Together
weeks.keyText: Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works,
weeks.theme: Gathering is not about checking in but about caring for one another; online or in person, we live out real body life.
group: In Hebrews 10:19-25, what grounds of grace come before the command not to forsake our assembling together?
When are you most likely to stop attending? What do you need most at those times?
As a small group, think of a member who hasn’t been around for a while. Who will reach out to them this week, and how?
weeks.sunday: Before you head out (or open the livestream), pray for one person you want to encourage. During the service, notice who is missing and who looks worn out. Afterward, say at least one specific word of encouragement to someone, or send a message to a member who didn’t come today: “Missed you.”

lessons.title: A New and Living Way
lessons.hear:
“Not forsaking our own assembling together” (Hebrews 10:25) is often used as a slogan to push people into the pews. But pull it out of its context and it becomes a cold rule. The writer of Hebrews actually lays out a long stretch of grace before he ever gives this command.

He says we have “boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19). In Old Testament times, only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, once a year, and only with blood. Now Jesus has opened for us “a new and living way” through his own body. This is the great door of the gospel: everyone who believes can come boldly before God.

Then the writer gives three exhortations, each one reaching further outward. First, “let’s draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith”—this is upward, our relationship with God. Second, “let’s hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering”—this is inward, our own faith. Third, “Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works” (Hebrews 10:24)—this is outward, our relationship with the body. “Not forsaking our own assembling together” sits inside that third exhortation.

So the purpose of gathering is not only for me to receive; it is about “one another”: caring for one another, stirring one another up, encouraging one another. To “consider” one another carries the sense of paying close attention and thinking carefully—keeping another person on your heart and pondering how to help them. That takes face-to-face time. It requires knowing one another’s names and stories.

The writer also mentions that some had already made it “the custom” to stay away. Leaving the fellowship is rarely a decision made in a single day; it is a habit formed slowly. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you: the way between me and God has been opened—am I also willing to walk in among my brothers and sisters?
lessons.light: In our relationships, the order is God first, then ourselves, then others. This passage follows exactly that order: draw near boldly to God, hold fast our own hope, and then consider one another. Gathering is not an add-on to faith but the natural flow of new life; selfless people keep their brothers and sisters on their hearts.
think: What are the three exhortations (“let’s …”) in Hebrews 10:19-25?
When I attend a gathering, do I think more about “me” or about “one another”?
Which member will I keep on my heart this week, thinking carefully about their needs?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for opening a new and living way for me through your own body, so that I can come boldly before the Father. Lead me toward my brothers and sisters too. Let me gather not only for myself, but learn to consider others and stir up love. Keep me from making it my custom to stay away. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the name of someone from your small group or church and spend five minutes thinking: What might they need right now? Pray for them, and look for a chance to show them care at the next gathering.
lessons.quick: The way to God is open; now I walk in among my brothers and sisters.
text: Having therefore, brothers, boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus,
by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh,
and having a great priest over God’s house,
let’s draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and having our body washed with pure water,
let’s hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering; for he who promised is faithful.
Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works,
not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.

lessons.title: Isn’t the Livestream Enough?
lessons.hear:
During the pandemic, one brother began watching the Sunday livestream at home. At first he took it seriously: he got dressed and sang along with his wife. Six months later, the livestream had become background noise for breakfast. A year later, he forgot to turn it on at all. When the church resumed in-person services, he said, “Online counts as church too. Faith is between me and God.” It wasn’t until his father passed away that he realized there wasn’t a single brother in his phone he could call.

In the same church was an elderly sister with limited mobility who turned on her camera every week, right on time, for the online small group. She remembered everyone’s prayer requests and often wrote in the chat, “I prayed for you today.” Everyone said she was the most “present” person in the group.

So the issue is not online versus in person; it is whether there is real body life. This is what the early church looked like: “They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer” (Acts 2:42). “Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home” (Acts 2:46)—they had large gatherings and small gatherings in homes; they listened to teaching and they ate together. Their faith was communal and visible.

Our old mindset says, “Faith is my personal business; church is an optional extra.” God’s view is that faith is personal, but it is never solitary. Salvation brings us to God one by one, and at the same time places us into a family.

So if illness, shift work, or living far away keeps you from attending in person, online is your channel of grace. You don’t need to feel second-class; just do your best to let yourself be known, and to get to know others. But if you are able to go out, and online has become a way of avoiding people, then ask yourself honestly: Am I participating in the body, or just watching it?
lessons.light: Self-centered faith says, “God and I are enough.” It sounds spiritual, but it often means not wanting to be bothered or known. The selfless life is willing to be placed into the body, to receive others’ care and to carry others’ burdens. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than convenience.
think: In Acts 2:42-47, what elements made up the early believers’ gatherings?
When I attend online or in person, am I participating or just watching?
What one thing can I do to let myself be known at church?
lessons.speak: Father, forgive me for treating my faith as my own private business and letting convenience replace commitment. Thank you for providing online channels for members who cannot leave home, and keep me from abusing that convenience. Lead me into real body life, where I am known and where I come to know others. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If you usually attend online, turn on your camera this week, or greet a member by name in the chat. If you attend in person, invite someone to lunch after the service.
lessons.quick: Online or in person is fine; what matters is participating in the body, not watching it.
text: They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.
Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles.
All who believed were together, and had all things in common.
They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.
Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.

lessons.title: While It Is Called “Today”
lessons.hear:
Elsewhere the writer of Hebrews says, “but exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called ‘today,’ lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). A heart rarely hardens overnight. It is like a loaf of bread left out on the counter, going stale a little more each day. The writer’s remedy is to “exhort one another day by day.”

To exhort is not to lecture. It is to come alongside, to give someone a hand, to speak a word that carries strength. You can start practicing this kind of mutual care today, whether on Sunday, in small group, or in an online gathering. First, before the gathering, choose one member and pray for them, asking the Lord to show you their needs. Second, during the gathering, pay attention to them, and also notice who is missing; online, notice who hasn’t spoken in a long time or who logs off early. Third, after the gathering, go find them and give a specific word of encouragement: “What you shared today really helped me.” Or message someone who was absent: “Missed you today. Is there anything I can pray about for you?”

Jesus promised, “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them” (Matthew 18:20). The context of that verse is about correcting and restoring a brother. The Lord is present not only where there is a pulpit and a microphone, but wherever two or three care for one another and pray for one another.

The Teacher in the Old Testament also said, “Two are better than one,” because “if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow” (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). A small greeting may be the sip of warm water that keeps a heart from hardening. Don’t wait until someone has left the church to say, “I wish I had checked in on them.” Do it while it is still called “today.”
lessons.light: Practicing 920 begins with the “2” beside us: everyone who gathers with me is a “2” God has placed at my side. Selfless people don’t just pay attention to their own feelings at church; they also notice the look in other people’s eyes. This is where stirring one another up to love and good works begins.
think: According to Ecclesiastes 4:9-12, why are two better than one?
Is there a member who has been slowly growing cold, and I have never said anything?
To whom will I give a specific word of encouragement today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for promising to be present wherever two or three gather in your name. Open my eyes to see the weary and the absent at our gatherings. Give me courage and gentleness to speak a word of support while it is still called “today.” In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, message a member who has recently been missing from church. Don’t ask why; just say, “Missed you. I prayed for you. Let me know if there’s anything you need.”
lessons.quick: While it is still called “today,” speak a word of support to a brother or sister.
text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

lessons.title: The Day Thomas Wasn’t There
lessons.hear:
On the evening the risen Lord first appeared to his disciples, one of them was missing: Thomas “wasn’t with them when Jesus came” (John 20:24). We don’t know why he was absent. Perhaps his disappointment ran too deep; perhaps he was afraid; perhaps he just wanted to be alone. Whatever the reason, he missed the peace of that evening and the joy everyone shared.

Thomas’s response was honest: unless I see it with my own eyes and touch it with my own hands, I will not believe. Many who stop attending church carry a similar sentence in their hearts: “Unless the church changes first, I’m not going back.” “Unless that person apologizes, I’m not going back.”

Today, take time to review: What has caused me to stop attending in the past? Busyness? Exhaustion? Disappointment in people? Or a sin in my heart that I don’t want to face? Sometimes stopping is an expression of a self-centered life—I want to decide on my own terms, by my own schedule, according to my own comfort.

But we must also say honestly: some people leave because they were genuinely harmed in the church. If you have suffered spiritual abuse, verbal or physical harm, or any kind of mistreatment, what you need is not to be scolded for “not attending,” but to be protected and listened to. Please seek out a trusted pastor, your church’s denominational or oversight body, or professional help. You can begin again in a safe community.

The most moving line comes next: “After eight days again his disciples were inside and Thomas was with them” (John 20:26). The Lord did not leave Thomas outside the door. He appeared again when the brothers were gathered. Thomas came back to them, met the Lord right there, and made the fullest confession of all: “My Lord and my God!”

The first step of adjustment is often simply coming back. You don’t have to wait until you feel completely better, or until every question is resolved. Come back with your questions, and the Lord will meet you among your brothers and sisters.
lessons.light: Self-centered people say, “I’ll go back only on my terms.” Selfless people say, “Lord, I’m coming back with my questions.” Humility means laying down the conditions we have set and returning to our proper place as members of the body. But selflessness does not mean enduring harm; people matter more than tasks, and the church must all the more become a place where the wounded can safely return.
think: What did Thomas’s absence bring about, and what did his return bring about?
What has made me want to stop attending? What was the “unless” in my heart then?
How can I help a member on the margins feel safe to come back?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you did not give up on Thomas, and you have not given up on me. Forgive me for deciding on my own terms whether to return to your house. If there are wounds in my heart, heal them, and lead me to safe help; if there is pride in my heart, break it. Bring me back among my brothers and sisters, and meet me there. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down one “unless” that once made you want to stop attending, and bring it to the Lord in prayer. If there is harm in your heart that needs attention, arrange this week to talk with a trusted pastor or ministry leader.
lessons.quick: The first step of adjustment is often simply coming back.
text: But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, wasn’t with them when Jesus came.

The other disciples therefore said to him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”
After eight days, again his disciples were inside and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, the doors being locked, and stood in the middle, and said, “Peace be to you.”
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

lessons.title: Let’s Go to the LORD’s House
lessons.hear:
“I was glad when they said to me, ‘Let’s go to the LORD’s house!’” (Psalm 122:1). This is a Song of Ascents. Each year the Israelites traveled up to Jerusalem from all over the land for the feasts, singing as they walked. Notice how the first line begins: “when they said to me.” The psalmist’s gladness started with someone’s invitation.

This week we have seen that the ground of our gathering is the new way Jesus opened, and its purpose is to consider one another. We have thought through online and in-person gatherings, and we have honestly faced the reasons we stop attending. Now let’s become the people who say it to others.

Many people come back to church not because they saw a poster, but because someone said, “Shall we go together next week? I’ll wait for you at the door.” And many people stay in church not because the programs are impressive, but because someone remembers their name.

The psalmist goes on: “Jerusalem is built as a city that is compact together” (Psalm 122:3). Gathering joined the scattered tribes together, like stones fitted into a city. The church today is the same: brothers online and sisters in person, old and young, new believers and seasoned ones—all are joined together by the Lord.

Finally, the psalmist blesses the city: “For my brothers’ and companions’ sakes, I will now say, ‘Peace be within you’” (Psalm 122:8). He loved gathering because he loved his brothers and companions. That is the driving force of multiplication—not boosting attendance numbers, but loving people and therefore inviting them to come before the Lord with us.

This week, find a spiritual companion and pray together for the peace of your church. Then each of you invite one friend who hasn’t come in a long time, or who doesn’t yet have a church, to join you.
lessons.light: The first step of 235 is to become spiritual companions with someone who lives the selfless life. When two companions pray together for their church and invite people together, multiplication has begun. If the truth stays only with me, gathering is just my habit; when it is passed on, gathering becomes home for many more.
think: In Psalm 122, why was the psalmist glad to go to the LORD’s house?
Who first invited me into church life and walked with me?
Whom will I ask this week to go to church with me?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for bringing me into your house through someone else’s invitation. Make me someone who invites others too. I pray for the peace of my church: may we be joined closely together, may members online and in person all be loved and known, and may many more be glad to come before you because of our love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, set aside five minutes with your spiritual companion to pray together for the peace of your church. Then each of you invite a friend to join you this Sunday (in person or online), and agree on a time and place.
lessons.quick: Be the one who says, “Let’s go to the LORD’s house.”
text: I was glad when they said to me, “Let’s go to the LORD’s house!”
Our feet are standing within your gates, Jerusalem!
Jerusalem is built as a city that is compact together,
where the tribes go up, even the LORD’s tribes, according to an ordinance for Israel, to give thanks to the LORD’s name.
For there are set thrones for judgment, the thrones of David’s house.
Pray for the peace of Jerusalem. Those who love you will prosper.
Peace be within your walls, and prosperity within your palaces.
For my brothers’ and companions’ sakes, I will now say, “Peace be within you.”
For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your good.

weeks.title: Baptism and Communion: United with Christ and His Body
weeks.keyText: Because there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf of bread.
weeks.theme: Baptism places me into Christ, and Communion gathers us at one table; united with the Lord, we are united with one another.
group: According to 1 Corinthians 10:16-17, what is the result of sharing in one loaf?
Share about your baptism or your first time taking Communion. If you haven’t yet, what hesitations do you have?
Before your next Communion, is there someone you need to be reconciled with? As the group prays for one another, what one step will each of you commit to?
weeks.sunday: If there is Communion this Sunday, read the passage where the Lord instituted the Supper quietly the night before and examine yourself. If someone comes to mind with whom you need to be reconciled, deal with it before the Lord first, and as far as possible take the first step. As you receive the bread and cup, look at the members around you: we share one loaf. If there is no Communion, remember your own baptism and pray for someone who is preparing to be baptized.

lessons.title: One Loaf, One Body
lessons.hear:
Before Jesus ascended, he did not leave behind a building or an organizational chart. He left two signs we can see and touch: baptism and the Lord’s Supper. He commanded his disciples, “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). And on the night he was betrayed, he took bread and said, “Do this in memory of me” (1 Corinthians 11:24).

Throughout church history, these two practices have been understood in many different ways. Some traditions call them sacraments; others call them ordinances. Baptism may be by sprinkling, pouring, or immersion; some churches baptize infants, while others baptize only those who can confess faith for themselves. Denominations also differ on how the Lord is present in Communion. These differences deserve respect and careful study, and you can ask your own pastor what your church teaches. Here we will not rank one above another; instead, we will look together at the core that churches everywhere hold in common.

That core is in today’s passage: “Because there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf of bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17). Paul calls the bread “a sharing of the body of Christ.” This word “sharing” means fellowship, participation, having a part in something. When we receive the bread and the cup, we have a share in Christ, and at the same time we share life with everyone who receives alongside us.

Baptism is the same. Paul says, “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13). Baptism is not only my personal testimony; it is also the sign that I have been placed into the body.

So both of these practices have a vertical line and a horizontal line. The vertical line is my union with Christ; the horizontal line is my union with my brothers and sisters. With only the vertical line, they become private religious experiences; with only the horizontal line, they become mere group activities. And the cross is exactly where those two lines meet.
lessons.light: Baptism and Communion turn truth into visible signs: I no longer belong to myself but to Christ, and to his body. Self-centered people treat these practices as personal spiritual experiences; selfless people see the Lord in the bread and the cup, and also see the people sharing it beside them. Letting Jesus reign begins with confessing, “We are one loaf.”
think: In 1 Corinthians 10:16-17, what two relationships does “sharing” bring out?
In the past, have I emphasized the vertical line or the horizontal line in baptism and Communion?
Next time I take Communion, how will I both remember the Lord and see the members around me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for giving us baptism and Communion, so that even my body can remember your grace. Small as I am, I have been placed into your body; many as we are, we are one loaf. Help me respect brothers and sisters from different traditions, while holding tightly to our unity in you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask a fellow believer from a different church background, “How does your church practice Communion or baptism? What does it mean to you?” Listen carefully without debating, and finish by thanking the Lord together.
lessons.quick: We, who are many, are one loaf and one body.
text: The cup of blessing which we bless, isn’t it a sharing of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, isn’t it a sharing of the body of Christ?
Because there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf of bread.

lessons.title: Baptism Is Not a Diploma
lessons.hear:
A young brother in a small group had been a believer for three years but still hadn’t been baptized. When asked why, he said, “I’m not good enough yet. I’ll get baptized once I’ve gotten rid of all my bad habits.” A sister in the same group was the opposite. She had been baptized as a teenager and could barely remember the day: “It was just a ceremony. Once it’s done, it’s done.”

These two views treat baptism either as a diploma—something you receive only after earning all your credits—or as an admission ticket you can throw away once you’re through the door. Paul’s view is entirely different: “We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4).

Baptism does not announce, “I’m already good.” It announces, “I have died”—my old self was crucified with Christ—and “I have come alive”—I have new life in Christ. It is not my achievement but Christ’s achievement stamped upon me. So you don’t need to wait until you are good enough to be baptized. When the Ethiopian eunuch heard the gospel and saw water, he asked, “What is keeping me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36). Of course, churches have different ways of preparing seekers for baptism; those are a help, not a hurdle.

To those already baptized, Paul says, “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:11). “Consider yourselves” is a daily discipline. The day of your baptism is not the finish line but the starting point of a lifelong identity. When temptation comes, you can say to yourself, “That old self has already been buried with Christ.”

That young brother eventually understood, and he was baptized on an Easter Sunday. He said, “I’m not being baptized because I’ve become good. Baptism reminds me that I already belong to him—so I can begin to change.”
lessons.light: Self-centered people put their own performance at the center: “Am I good enough?” The selfless life puts Christ’s accomplishment at the center: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20). Baptism is the very sign of selflessness: the old self has been buried. When I consider myself alive to God, my daily living follows.
think: In Romans 6:3-11, how is baptism related to Christ’s death and resurrection?
Do I see baptism as a diploma, an admission ticket, or the starting point of an identity?
In what one area today will I “consider myself dead to sin”?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that in Christ I have died with him, been buried with him, and been raised with him. Forgive me for thinking I had to be good enough on my own, and forgive me for forgetting what my baptism means. Today I declare: my old self has been crucified, and in Christ I am alive to you. Holy Spirit, help me walk in newness of life. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If you have been baptized, write down the date of your baptism and how you felt that day, and share it with a fellow member. If you haven’t, reach out this week to your pastor or small group leader to talk about your hesitations.
lessons.quick: Baptism doesn’t say I’m already good; it says my old self has died and I live in Christ.
text: Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?
We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.
For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will also be part of his resurrection;
knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.
For he who has died has been freed from sin.
But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him,
knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more. Death no longer has dominion over him!
For the death that he died, he died to sin one time; but the life that he lives, he lives to God.
Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

lessons.title: Remember, Proclaim, Await
lessons.hear:
When Paul speaks about the Lord’s Supper, he uses a weighty word: “delivered.” He says, “For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you” (1 Corinthians 11:23). Communion has been handed down from the hands of the Lord Jesus, generation after generation—through eras of persecution, underground gatherings, wars, and plagues—until today it has been placed in your hands.

This passage gives us three directions for receiving Communion, and they are also directions we can practice today. First, look back: remember. “Do this in memory of me.” Remembering is more than recalling; it lets that night become my present: the Lord’s body given for me, the Lord’s blood poured out for me. Second, look around: proclaim. “For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death” (1 Corinthians 11:26). Communion is a sermon without words, in which the whole congregation declares to the world together: our hope is in the cross. Third, look ahead: await. “Until he comes.” Every time we receive Communion, we are getting a foretaste of the coming feast; the Lord said he would drink it new with us in his Father’s kingdom (see Matthew 26:29).

The psalmist invites us, “Oh taste and see that the LORD is good” (Psalm 34:8). Communion is an experience of tasting: grace is not only heard with the ears but received with the hands and tasted with the mouth.

Today’s practice is to carry these three directions into daily life. Look back, and write down how the Lord’s grace saved you. Look around, and think about who usually sits beside you at Communion and what they might need from you. Look ahead, and view the members who are still struggling with eyes of hope. If your church celebrates Communion once a month, why not start preparing this week? If you join online, follow your church’s guidance and take part in the remembrance wholeheartedly.
lessons.light: The final step on the Way of Service is “God”: all glory to God, giving thanks in everything. When the Lord instituted the Supper, he took the bread and first “gave thanks,” which is why some traditions call Communion the Eucharist, the feast of thanksgiving. When I remember that the Lord gave his body for me, I no longer live for myself, and I become willing to lay down my life for the members who share the table with me.
think: In 1 Corinthians 11:23-26, what are the three time directions of Communion?
When I receive Communion, what am I usually thinking about?
Before my next Communion, which member who shares the table with me will I pray for?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, your body was given for me and your blood was poured out for me; I will remember you. Each time I receive Communion, let me taste your goodness afresh, proclaim your death with my life, and await your return with hope. Help me see the members at the table with me and love them as you have loved me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact a member who was recently baptized or is preparing for baptism. Tell them you thank God for them, and share one line that moves you most when you take Communion.
lessons.quick: Look back and remember, look around and proclaim, look ahead and await the Lord’s return.
text: For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread.
When he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.”
In the same way he also took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me.”
For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

lessons.title: Examine Yourself, Then Eat
lessons.hear:
Many people become afraid when they read about eating the bread or drinking the Lord’s cup “in a way unworthy of the Lord.” Some have not dared to take Communion for years because they feel unworthy. But if you read what comes before, you will find that Paul was not rebuking the Corinthian church for being imperfect. He was rebuking them for dividing into factions at the Lord’s table: the wealthy ate and drank first, some even getting drunk, while poorer brothers who rushed in after work found the table already bare. Paul said that in this way, “it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat” (1 Corinthians 11:20).

So “not discerning the Lord’s body” can be examined from two sides. On one side, it means taking lightly the body the Lord gave for me, treating the cross as a small thing. On the other, it means looking down on the Lord’s body—the church—and despising the brothers and sisters around me. Paul’s remedy is this: “But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread, and drink of the cup” (1 Corinthians 11:28). Notice that he says “and so let him eat,” not “and so let him stay away.” The purpose of self-examination is to bring us to the table, not to keep us from it.

You can examine yourself with three questions: Is there sin I am hiding from the Lord? Am I looking down on any member of the body? Is there a relationship that needs reconciliation that I keep putting off? Jesus said, “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24).

We should also say gently: reconciliation takes two people. What you can do is take your own step as fully as you can—admit your wrong, apologize, let go of resentment. If the other person does not respond, or if the relationship involves harm or is unsafe, forgiveness does not mean you must immediately restore trust. You can entrust it to the Lord and seek help from a pastor or a professional.

The most beautiful restoration also happened beside a meal. On the night the Supper was instituted, Peter denied the Lord three times. After the resurrection, Jesus prepared breakfast for him on the shore, and only after they had eaten did he ask, “Do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15). The Lord welcomed back a failed disciple with a meal. Self-examination is not meant to drive you away from the table, but to bring you back to it.
lessons.light: When self-centered people come to Communion, they look only at themselves—“Am I worthy?”—or don’t look at themselves at all. Selfless people see three directions at the table: they see the Lord, they see their own sin, and they see the members around them. Humility inspires humility: one person who takes the first step toward reconciliation can often bring healing to the whole body.
think: What behavior at the Lord’s Supper did Paul rebuke the Corinthians for?
Is there a member in my heart whom I look down on, or with whom I have not yet reconciled?
What small step can I take this week to do my part toward reconciliation?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, on the night you were betrayed, you still broke bread for your disciples. I am not worthy, yet by your grace I am invited to the table. Search me and show me my hidden sins and any contempt in my heart toward others. Give me courage to take the first step toward reconciliation, and wisdom to know when I need to seek help. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Take ten quiet minutes today to examine yourself, and write down one relationship that needs repair. If it is appropriate and safe, send a word of apology or a greeting this week; if it is not safe, arrange to talk with a pastor first.
lessons.quick: Self-examination is not meant to keep us from the table, but to bring us back to it.
text: Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s cup in a way unworthy of the Lord will be guilty of the body and the blood of the Lord.
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup.
For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy way eats and drinks judgment to himself if he doesn’t discern the Lord’s body.
For this cause many among you are weak and sickly, and not a few sleep.
For if we discerned ourselves, we wouldn’t be judged.
But when we are judged, we are disciplined by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with the world.

lessons.title: Recognized in the Breaking of the Bread
lessons.hear:
On the evening of resurrection day, two discouraged disciples were walking the road to Emmaus. Jesus walked with them and explained the Scriptures to them. Their hearts burned within them, yet they still did not recognize him—until they sat down to eat: “he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them. Their eyes were opened and they recognized him” (Luke 24:30-31).

Took, gave thanks, broke, gave—these actions echo the very actions of the night the Supper was instituted. In the breaking of the bread, they recognized the Lord. What happened next matters even more: “They rose up that very hour, returned to Jerusalem” (Luke 24:33), and told everything that had happened along the way and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread. People who have met the Lord will travel through the night to tell others.

This week we have seen that baptism unites us with Christ in his death and life, and that Communion makes us one loaf. We have learned to remember, proclaim, and await at the table, and to examine ourselves and seek reconciliation. Now let’s pass on what we have received.

The Old Testament Passover had a beautiful design. God told his people in advance, “It will happen, when your children ask you, ‘What do you mean by this service?’” (Exodus 12:26), that the parents were to tell the next generation the story of God’s deliverance. The ceremony itself is an invitation, waiting to be asked about and explained.

So the next time your church holds a baptism or Communion, sit with your children, a seeker friend, or a new believer. If they ask, “What does this mean?”, answer in your own words: “It means Jesus gave his body for us; we all belong to him, and we belong to one another.” A simple answer may be the moment another person’s eyes are opened.
lessons.light: The last step of changing a mindset is multiplication. Baptism and Communion are themselves the gospel handed down through the generations: from the Lord to the apostles, and from the apostles to us. The second relationship in 235 is spiritual parents and children; walking with a new believer until they understand what these practices mean is raising up the next spiritual generation.
think: When did the disciples on the road to Emmaus recognize the Lord, and what did they do after they recognized him?
Have I ever had an “eyes opened” moment at a baptism or Communion?
To whom will I explain the meaning of baptism or Communion?
lessons.speak: Risen Lord, thank you for walking with me on my road of discouragement and letting me recognize you in the breaking of the bread. Make me like the disciples of Emmaus, who rose at once to tell others after meeting you. Give me simple, clear words to pass on the meaning of baptism and Communion to the next generation and to new believers. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, find a child, a seeker friend, or a new believer, and take five minutes to share in your own words what baptism or Communion means to you. Invite them to come with you next time.
lessons.quick: Those who meet the Lord in the breaking of the bread rise up to tell others.
text: They came near to the village where they were going, and he acted like he would go further.
They urged him, saying, “Stay with us, for it is almost evening, and the day is almost over.” He went in to stay with them.
When he had sat down at the table with them, he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them.
Their eyes were opened and they recognized him; then he vanished out of their sight.
They said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?”
They rose up that very hour, returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them,
saying, “The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!”
They related the things that happened along the way, and how he was recognized by them in the breaking of the bread.

weeks.title: Everything Belongs to God: Our Identity as Stewards
weeks.keyText: But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.
weeks.theme: Nothing in my hands is truly mine; it is entrusted to me by God—I am a steward, not an owner.
group: Read 1 Chronicles 29:10-16. How did David view the people’s offering?
Among your time, money, and gifts, which is hardest for you to admit “belongs to God”?
This week, how will each of you use one thing “God has entrusted to you” to serve a fellow member, so you can share about it at the next small group?
weeks.sunday: Before you head out, look at your keys, your wallet, and your phone, and pray silently, “Lord, these are all yours.” When you give your offering during the service, don’t think about the amount first; first acknowledge that you are a steward. After the service, ask the Lord: This week, with what you have entrusted to me, whom do you want me to bless?

lessons.title: We Give You of Your Own
lessons.hear:
David’s greatest desire in his later years was to build a house for God. God did not let him build it with his own hands, so he set aside the gold, silver, and precious stones he had gathered over many years, and invited all the leaders to give as well. That day, the people rejoiced because they had given so willingly. By ordinary standards, it was the perfect moment for an awards ceremony and names engraved on a plaque.

Instead, David prayed before the whole assembly and gave all the credit back to God: “But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own” (1 Chronicles 29:14).

That sentence completely changes the meaning of giving. We usually think giving means “taking part of what is mine and handing it to God.” David says giving means “returning to God part of what is already God’s.” It is like a child using the allowance Dad gave him to buy Dad a present. Dad is delighted—not because of what the present cost, but because of the child’s heart.

Where did David get this perspective? From knowing God: “Yours, LORD, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and on the earth is yours.” (1 Chronicles 29:11). The psalm says the same: “The earth is the LORD’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it” (Psalm 24:1). Even we ourselves are included among “those who dwell in it.”

So our identity as stewards doesn’t begin with money. It begins with a reversal of mindset: from “mine” to “God’s.” My time, my body, my abilities, my home, my savings, even my family—all of them are entrusted to me by God for a season. David also said, “For we are strangers before you and foreigners” (1 Chronicles 29:15). We are travelers who can take nothing with us; we are stewards who will one day give an account.

This is not a heavy burden but a kind of freedom. Since everything belongs to God, I don’t have to clutch it tightly, and I don’t have to panic when I lose it.
lessons.light: The root of the self-centered life is treating what is God’s as mine and wanting to be the owner of my own life; this is precisely leaving our proper place as human beings and grasping power that belongs to God. Humility is returning to our proper place as stewards: God is the owner, and I am the one entrusted. Let Jesus reign—over the wallet, the calendar, and the front door.
think: In his prayer, what did David attribute to God?
What do I most often call “mine”?
In what one matter today can I say, “Lord, this is yours”?
lessons.speak: Father, all things come from you, and everything I have is your gift. Forgive me for so often treating what you have entrusted to me as my own, clutching it tightly and worrying over it. Today I place my time, my body, my money, and my home in your hands. I am your steward; teach me to be faithful. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, list on paper the five things you treasure most (such as time, home, children, abilities, savings). After each one write “the Lord’s,” and pray one sentence of surrender over each.
lessons.quick: From “mine” to “God’s”: I am a steward, not an owner.
text: Therefore David blessed the LORD before all the assembly; and David said, “You are blessed, LORD, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever.

Yours, LORD, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and on the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, LORD, and you are exalted as head above all.
Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all! In your hand is power and might! It is in your hand to make great, and to give strength to all!
Now therefore, our God, we thank you and praise your glorious name.
But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.
For we are strangers before you and foreigners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is no remaining.
LORD our God, all this store that we have prepared to build you a house for your holy name comes from your hand, and is all your own.

lessons.title: Everything You Have Was Received
lessons.hear:
During a small group sharing time, a self-made brother said, “I built my business penny by penny with my own hands. A tenth goes to the church; the rest is mine, and it’s up to me how I use it.” The group fell silent for a moment. Then a sister added, “I don’t have much money, but my weekends are mine. It’s hard enough to get any rest—please don’t ask me to serve.”

Those two statements represent a very common old mindset: I own it first, then I pick a portion for God. God’s view is that everything already belongs to him, and I am the one entrusted to manage it.

Paul asked the Corinthian church a pointed question: “And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). The Corinthians prided themselves on their gifts, their eloquence, and which famous teacher they followed. Paul reminded them that everything they boasted about had been received.

Moses had warned the Israelites long before. Once they entered the good land and had eaten their fill, they were to beware of saying in their hearts, “My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:17). He went on to remind them that it is God who gives the power to get wealth. Your health, your mind, your opportunities, the family you were born into, the people who opened doors for you—which of these did you create yourself? Hard work is real, but the very ability to work hard is grace.

So what is a steward’s most important qualification? “It is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2). It is not how much they own, but whether they are faithful with what has been entrusted to them.

Later, that brother was deeply moved by this verse at a retreat. He said, “I used to ask, ‘How much should I give God?’ Now I ask, ‘How does God want me to use this money of his?’” When the question changed, his life changed too. He began using his company’s resources to host internships for the church’s young people, and he set aside part of his weekends for his family and his small group.
lessons.light: Change your perspective and you change your mindset: from “I own it, so I decide” to “God entrusted it, so I give an account.” This is a view from heaven rather than earth, from eternity rather than the moment. The identity of a steward tears down both pride and anxiety—I am not the owner, so I need not boast, and I need not fear.
think: In 1 Corinthians 4:1-7, how does Paul describe what is required of a steward?
Is there a “the rest is mine” zone in my heart?
In what area will I change my question from “how much do I give God” to “how does God want me to use this”?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that I often make too much of my own efforts and too little of your grace. What do I have that I didn’t receive? Forgive my boasting and my tight grip. Make me a faithful steward who asks for your heart in my finances, my time, and my gifts—not only for my own preferences. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, get together with your spiritual companion. Each of you name one thing you have always treated as your own, and pray for each other, asking the Lord to teach you to see it again through a steward’s eyes.
lessons.quick: What do I have that I didn’t receive? What is required of a steward is faithfulness.
text: So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants and stewards of God’s mysteries.
Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by a human court. Yes, I don’t even judge my own self.
For I know nothing against myself. Yet I am not justified by this, but he who judges me is the Lord.

Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of the hearts. Then each man will get his praise from God.

Now these things, brothers, I have in a figure transferred to myself and Apollos for your sakes, that in us you might learn not to think beyond the things which are written, that none of you be puffed up against one another.
For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?

lessons.title: Good Managers of God’s Many-Colored Grace
lessons.hear:
When people hear the word “steward,” many think first of money. But Peter’s scope is much wider: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms” (1 Peter 4:10). “In its various forms” carries the sense of many-colored, like a piece of cloth woven with many colors. What God has entrusted to you might be a good singing voice, a gift for cooking, a car, a living room, hands that can fix computers, ears willing to listen, or a testimony of coming through failure.

Notice the direction of this verse: “serving one another.” A gift is not a trophy for you to keep on a shelf; it is bread for you to hand out. A steward holds the master’s keys not to lock up the storehouse, but to give the household their portion of food at the right time.

In the verse just before, Peter says, “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (1 Peter 4:9). In the early church, opening your home to welcome fellow believers was the most common act of stewardship. It is the same in Chinese churches today: a home-cooked meal, a ride on your way, a weekend spent helping someone move—all of these are ways of managing God’s grace.

Today’s practice is very concrete. First, take stock: think of one thing you own or one ability you have. Next, aim it: think of a member who has a need right now—a family that just moved, an elderly person living alone, a young person looking for work. Then give it away: this week, use that one thing to serve them.

Paul also reminds us, “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Even our bodies belong to the Lord. When we use our bodies to drive someone, cook a meal, or visit someone, we are glorifying God in our bodies. Peter says the purpose of serving is “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ”—not that I am praised, but that he is seen.
lessons.light: Self-denial is for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. A gift used only for ourselves becomes a tool of the self-centered life; given away to serve others, it becomes a channel of the selfless life. People matter more than tasks: a good steward asks not only “How can this task be done well?” but even more “How can this person be blessed?”
think: What specific ways of serving are mentioned in 1 Peter 4:8-11?
What gift or resource do I have that I have never given away?
This week, what will I use to serve which member?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for entrusting me with your grace in its many forms; even my body is yours, bought at a great price. Open my eyes to see the resources in my hands and the needs around me. Lead me this week to use what you have given me to serve one of your people, so that you may be glorified in all things. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, choose a member who has a need, and serve them concretely with one of your gifts or resources (a meal, a ride, time spent together). Set a time with them today.
lessons.quick: A gift is not a trophy; it is bread given to me to hand out.
text: And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.
Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

lessons.title: Is the Master Delaying?
lessons.hear:
Jesus told a parable about stewards. The faithful steward gives the household “their portion of food at the right times.” The unfaithful steward says in his heart, “My lord delays his coming,” and begins to beat the menservants and maidservants and to eat, drink, and get drunk. Both held the same authority and resources; the difference came down to one thought: Will the master come back?

The unfaithful steward made two mistakes. First, he forgot that he was only a steward and began using the master’s goods to satisfy himself. Second, he forgot that the other servants were not his property and began to oppress them. This is something the church today must stay alert to: whether you are a small group leader, a ministry team member, a deacon, or a pastor, your position and resources are entrusted by the Lord—not for controlling people or serving yourself. If you encounter the abuse of power or money in the church, dealing with it through proper channels, a trusted third party, or your church’s denominational or oversight body is exactly how we answer to the true Master.

Today, review honestly: In what area am I living as if the master were delaying his coming? Perhaps I have put off a ministry I should be doing. Perhaps I treat church resources as my own convenience. Perhaps I no longer speak gently to my co-workers or my family. Jesus said, “To whomever much is given, of him will much be required; and to whom much was entrusted, of him more will be asked” (Luke 12:48).

The Gospels also tell a story of restoration. Zacchaeus the tax collector was a man who clutched everything in his hands, even using his position to cheat others. When Jesus came to his house as a guest, his heart turned around: “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much” (Luke 19:8). No one forced him, yet he gladly went from “owner” back to steward. Jesus declared, “Today, salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9).

The way to adjust is not to grip more tightly but to let go more completely. When Jesus comes into our homes, our account books, and our calendars, the heart of a steward begins to grow again.
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our proper place and grasping power: when a steward wants to be the owner, he ends up oppressing his fellow servants. Humility is laying down power and returning to our proper place: remembering that the Master may return at any moment, and that our fellow servants all belong to the Lord. Zacchaeus’s turnaround shows us that once a life is touched by grace, it opens its hands freely.
think: In Luke 12:42-48, what is the difference between the faithful and the unfaithful steward?
In what area am I living as if “my lord delays his coming”?
Like Zacchaeus, in what specific matter will I let go or make amends?
lessons.speak: Lord, you may return at any moment, yet I often live as though you are a long way off. Forgive me for using the position and resources you entrusted to me to satisfy myself, and even for hurting the people around me. Come into my heart as you came into Zacchaeus’s house, and make me glad to let go and willing to make amends, so that I become a faithful steward again. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down one trust you have put off or handled unfaithfully (a ministry, a sum of money, a block of time), and take one corrective action today. If you have wronged a fellow member, go and apologize to them.
lessons.quick: The Master may return at any moment; a faithful steward feeds the household and does not oppress his fellow servants.
text: The Lord said, “Who then is the faithful and wise steward, whom his lord will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the right times?
Blessed is that servant whom his lord will find doing so when he comes.
Truly I tell you that he will set him over all that he has.
But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My lord delays his coming,’ and begins to beat the menservants and the maidservants, and to eat and drink and to be drunken,
then the lord of that servant will come in a day when he isn’t expecting him and in an hour that he doesn’t know, and will cut him in two, and place his portion with the unfaithful.
That servant who knew his lord’s will, and didn’t prepare nor do what he wanted, will be beaten with many stripes,

but he who didn’t know, and did things worthy of stripes, will be beaten with few stripes. To whomever much is given, of him will much be required; and to whom much was entrusted, of him more will be asked.

lessons.title: Good and Faithful Servant
lessons.hear:
“Now after a long time the lord of those servants came, and settled accounts with them” (Matthew 25:19). Though the master in the parable was gone a long time, he was certain to return. This is the most sobering line in a steward’s life: one day we will all stand before the Lord and give an account of everything entrusted to us in this life.

But notice what the master says to the faithful servant: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25:21). The master did not compare five talents with two; both servants received word-for-word the same praise. God does not look at the numbers in your hands, but at your faithfulness. And the end of the accounting is not a cold report card, but “Enter into the joy of your lord”—it is a celebration.

This week, we learned from David’s prayer that “everything belongs to God,” from Paul’s question, “What do you have that you didn’t receive?”, and from Peter to serve one another with God’s grace in its many forms; and we saw in Zacchaeus the freedom of letting go.
