Now let’s pass on this identity as stewards.

The call to stewardship was placed on human beings from the very beginning. After God created man, “The LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). From the start, humans were never the owners of the garden, but its gardeners. Today we pass this calling on to the next generation: help your children divide their allowance into three portions—giving thanks, saving, and spending; pray with a new believer, “Lord, my time is yours”; share with your small group a real experience of being a steward, including both your failures and what you learned.

People who understand that they are stewards tend to be more generous, more free, and less anxious. When a church is full of such people, it becomes a visible corner of God’s kingdom on earth.
lessons.light: The “0” in 920 is the practice of selflessness: not treating what is God’s as mine. When I live out my identity as a steward, the fruit of the Spirit grows naturally: generosity, faithfulness, joy. Multiplication starts with the “2” beside me, living out the conviction that “everything belongs to God” before the next generation.
think: In Matthew 25:19-23, on what basis did the master praise his servants?
In what “few things” am I learning to be faithful this week?
To whom will I pass on the mindset of a steward, and how?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for giving me the garden to cultivate and keep, and for entrusting your house, your people, and your resources to me. Make me faithful in a few things, and help me pass this steward’s heart on to children and new believers. I long for the day when I will hear you say, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, sit down for ten minutes with a child or a new believer and share that “everything belongs to God.” Together, decide on one concrete act of stewardship (such as dividing an allowance or planning the week’s time).
lessons.quick: God looks not at the numbers but at faithfulness; the end of the accounting is a celebration.
text: “Now after a long time the lord of those servants came, and settled accounts with them.
He who received the five talents came and brought another five talents, saying, ‘Lord, you delivered to me five talents. Behold, I have gained another five talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
“He also who got the two talents came and said, ‘Lord, you delivered to me two talents. Behold, I have gained another two talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things. I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’

weeks.title: Cheerful Giving
weeks.keyText: Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
weeks.theme: Giving is not a membership fee demanded of us but a heart touched by grace, gladly responding to the Lord who became poor for our sake.
group: Read 2 Corinthians 8:1-9. How could the Macedonian churches give so gladly in the middle of deep poverty?
In the past, when you thought about giving, did you mostly feel burden, pressure, joy, or numbness? Why?
What quiet, low-key way could you bless a member of the body who is in need this week?
weeks.sunday: This Lord’s Day, before the offering, pause for a quiet moment and remember that the Lord Jesus, “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Whatever amount you give, give yourself to the Lord first. During the service, pay attention to the songs of thanksgiving; afterward, pray for the needs of the church and for the co-workers who handle the offerings.

lessons.title: Giving That Flows from Grace
lessons.hear:
Mention giving, and many people tense up a little. Some remember the appeals from the pulpit and the awkward moment the offering bag comes down the row; others think of off-putting slogans like “give and you’ll be blessed.” But when Paul talks about giving, his opening word is not “money” but “grace”: “Moreover, brothers, we make known to you the grace of God which has been given in the assemblies of Macedonia” (2 Corinthians 8:1).

The Macedonian churches were not wealthy. Paul describes how, “in a severe ordeal of affliction, the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded to the riches of their generosity” (2 Corinthians 8:2). Nobody had to coax or pressure them. On the contrary, they kept “begging us with much entreaty to receive this grace and the fellowship in the service to the saints” (2 Corinthians 8:4). To them, simply being allowed to give was itself a grace and an honor.

The secret is in verse 5: “first they gave their own selves to the Lord” (2 Corinthians 8:5). In giving, people come before possessions. What God wants has never been what is in our pockets; he wants all of us. Once the heart belongs to the Lord, the hand opens naturally.

And the source of it all is verse 9: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The cross is heaven’s greatest gift. We do not give in order to receive grace; we give because we have already received it. When David gathered materials for the temple, he said the same thing: “For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own” (1 Chronicles 29:14).

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you first what the Lord gave for you, and only then to look at what is in your hands.
lessons.light: The self-centered person looks at giving and counts “how much I am losing”; the selfless person looks at giving and sees “how much the Lord gave up for me.” Change your viewpoint and you change your mindset: from earth’s point of view, giving is an expense; from heaven’s, it is worship that answers grace. Give yourself to the Lord first, and let Jesus reign over your wallet too.
think: In 2 Corinthians 8:1-9, what marks the Macedonian churches’ attitude toward giving?
When I think about giving, what surfaces first in my heart: grace, pressure, or calculation?
How can I give myself to the Lord afresh today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you were rich, yet for my sake you became poor. I confess that I often calculate and hesitate when it comes to giving, and sometimes I give reluctantly. Holy Spirit, let me see your grace first, so that I give myself to you first, and then gladly place what I have in your hands as well. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Spend five quiet minutes today writing down three graces you have received from God but often take for granted (not just money). Thank the Lord for each one, then pray, “Lord, I give myself to you first.”
lessons.quick: We don’t give to receive grace; we give because we have already received it.
text: Moreover, brothers, we make known to you the grace of God which has been given in the assemblies of Macedonia,
how in a severe ordeal of affliction, the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded to the riches of their generosity.
For according to their power, I testify, yes and beyond their power, they gave of their own accord,
begging us with much entreaty to receive this grace and the fellowship in the service to the saints.
This was not as we had expected, but first they gave their own selves to the Lord, and to us through the will of God.
So we urged Titus, that as he had made a beginning before, so he would also complete in you this grace.
But as you abound in everything—in faith, utterance, knowledge, all earnestness, and in your love to us—see that you also abound in this grace.
I speak not by way of commandment, but as proving through the earnestness of others the sincerity also of your love.
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.

lessons.title: Gladly, Not Grudgingly
lessons.hear:
A sister who had been in church for many years felt her stomach knot up every time the offering came around. The church she grew up in used to read out the list of givers from the front, and harsh rebukes were common. She kept giving, but out of fear and guilt; at other times she swung the other way and put nothing in at all, only to feel even more uneasy. Then one day, reading this verse in her small group, she finally understood it for the first time: “Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

We tend to carry two old mindsets. One treats giving as a “membership fee,” money the church collects from me. The other treats it as an “investment”: the more I put in, the more I get back later. The first makes us grudging; the second makes us greedy. Both have wandered away from grace.

Paul uses the picture of sowing: “he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully” (2 Corinthians 9:6). But look at what the harvest is. “God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work” (2 Corinthians 9:8). God gives us enough not so we can hoard and indulge, but so we can keep on blessing others. The harvest is “the fruits of your righteousness” (2 Corinthians 9:10), and the end result is “thanksgiving to God” (2 Corinthians 9:11). This is not a “give and get rich” formula; it is how a generous heavenly Father raises generous children.

Many churches encourage believers to practice giving a tenth, and that can be a good starting point for putting God first. But it is not a condition for earning salvation or blessing. The New Testament’s focus is not on a percentage but on a heart: what God values is the honesty and gladness of giving “as he has determined in his heart.” You can be still before God, talk it over with him, and then give with joy.
lessons.light: Grudging giving is law; giving that calculates the return is a transaction. Both revolve around the self. Cheerful giving is selfless love: not to make a name for myself, not to buy a blessing, but only so that Jesus receives the glory. When I humbly admit that everything I have was received, my heart is set free.
think: According to 2 Corinthians 9:6-11, why does God give us all sufficiency?
Is my giving more like paying a membership fee, making an investment, or responding to grace?
How will I decide my giving before God “as I have determined in my heart”?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I have given out of fear, and I have also secretly hoped my giving would buy me some benefit. Set me free from compulsion and calculation, and help me know you as a generous Father. Teach me to give as I have determined in my heart, offering with joy what you have given me, so that thanks overflow to you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Find some quiet time tonight, alone or with your spouse, to review your giving before God. Don’t ask, “Is it enough?” Ask, “Is it glad?” Tell the Lord honestly how you feel and ask him to renew your heart.
lessons.quick: God doesn’t look at the number; he looks for a cheerful heart.
text: Remember this: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work.
As it is written, “He has scattered abroad. He has given to the poor. His righteousness remains forever.”
Now may he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, supply and multiply your seed for sowing, and increase the fruits of your righteousness,
you being enriched in everything for all generosity, which produces thanksgiving to God through us.

lessons.title: The Lord Sees Two Small Coins
lessons.hear:
Jesus “sat down opposite the treasury, and saw how the multitude cast money into the treasury” (Mark 12:41). The scene can make us a little uncomfortable: the Lord is watching. But he is not watching the amounts; he is watching the “how.” The rich put in a lot, and a widow put in just two small coins, yet Jesus said, “Most certainly I tell you, this poor widow gave more than all those who are giving into the treasury” (Mark 12:43).

In human bookkeeping, she gave the least; in God’s books, she gave the most. She was not handing over a little from her surplus; she was entrusting herself to God. This passage is not telling us to drop our whole living allowance into the offering box—Scripture also commands us to care for our families and live responsibly. Rather, it shows us that God treasures trust and love, and he never despises a small gift. Moses taught Israel long ago: “Every man shall give as he is able, according to the LORD your God’s blessing which he has given you” (Deuteronomy 16:17).

Giving doesn’t only happen in the offering bag on Sunday. In the early church, gifts were often meant to meet the shortfalls of fellow members so that there might be “equality” among them (see 2 Corinthians 8:13-14). Today’s exercise is to let a cheerful heart land on one real person in the body: perhaps a brother who just lost his job, a sister caring for a sick family member on her own, or an international student who has just arrived in your city. Buy them a meal, drop off a bag of groceries, cover a ride for them. Do it quietly, without fanfare, and without making them feel they owe you.

What you give may be only “two small coins,” but the Lord is sitting there, and he sees. For that member of the body, it is a sign that God remembers them; for you, it is a practice that flows from grace.
lessons.light: People matter more than things, and relationships matter more than possessions. Giving doesn’t end in a number; it ends in a person who is loved. When a cheerful heart lands on the “2” beside you, the 920 practice gains warmth. Give without fanfare and without condescension, and let the glory go to the Lord who sees.
think: In Mark 12:41-44, what standard does Jesus use to measure how much was given?
Do I think I don’t need to give because I “can’t give much”?
Which member of the body in need can I quietly bless today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for seeing the widow’s two small coins, and for seeing my small offerings too. Open my eyes to the brothers and sisters around me who are in need, and give me a cheerful heart to bless them quietly with what you have given me, not seeking to be noticed, only that you be glorified. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a brother or sister under financial or practical pressure right now, and bless them once today in a quiet way that won’t burden them: a meal, a bag of everyday groceries, or an encouragement card. Then pray for them.
lessons.quick: The Lord sits opposite the treasury, looking at hearts, not amounts.
text: Jesus sat down opposite the treasury and saw how the multitude cast money into the treasury. Many who were rich cast in much.
A poor widow came and she cast in two small brass coins, which equal a quadrans coin.
He called his disciples to himself and said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, this poor widow gave more than all those who are giving into the treasury,
for they all gave out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, gave all that she had to live on.”

lessons.title: The Motives Behind Our Giving
lessons.hear:
The story of Ananias and Sapphira is unsettling to read. They sold a piece of property, quietly kept back part of the money, and pretended they were giving it all. Peter’s words deserve a careful look: “While you kept it, didn’t it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power?” (Acts 5:4). They were never obligated to give it all; how much they gave was up to them. Their problem was not giving too little but wanting people to think they had given more—deceiving others for the sake of a spiritual reputation.

This mirror exposes several hidden forms of self-centeredness in our giving. First, giving to be seen. The Lord Jesus warns, “don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matthew 6:3). Second, using giving to buy influence: “I give the most, so my opinion should carry the most weight.” That is trying to reign in the church with money. Third, clutching tightly out of fear or stinginess: knowing full well that the Lord is prompting us, yet not daring to let go.

Some have seen offerings misused and have grown cold ever since. That kind of wound is real. A healthy church should be transparent and accountable with its finances and open to oversight. If you discover financial wrongdoing, you don’t have to stay silent; raise it through proper channels—the elders and deacons board, a denominational body, or a trustworthy third party. At the same time, ask the Lord for healing, so that one injury does not rob you of a cheerful heart.

The way of adjustment is plain to see in Zacchaeus. This once-greedy tax collector, after Jesus freely welcomed him, stood up on his own and said, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor” (Luke 19:8). No one forced him; grace opened his hand. Adjustment does not mean forcing ourselves harder; it means coming back to grace again.
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our proper place and grasping power; using giving to buy a voice is trying to reign in the church. Humility is laying down power and returning to our proper place: I am only a steward—the money is the Lord’s, and so is the church. After review comes not self-condemnation but letting grace open my hand once more.
think: In Acts 5:1-4, what was Ananias’s real problem?
Is any part of my giving about being seen or gaining influence?
How will I adjust so that my giving returns to simple love?
lessons.speak: Father, you search the heart. I confess that my giving is sometimes mixed with vanity, calculation, or fear. Forgive me and purify my motives. Heal the wounds I have suffered around money, and don’t let bitterness bind me. Like Zacchaeus, let your grace open my hand. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today write down the one thing in your giving that most needs adjusting (vanity, clutching, bitterness, or something else). Confess it to the Lord or entrust it to him, then write one concrete step—for example, spending one quiet minute in thanksgiving before you next give.
lessons.quick: God doesn’t want giving as a performance; he wants an honest heart opened by grace.
text: But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession,
and kept back part of the price, his wife also being aware of it, then brought a certain part and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back part of the price of the land?
While you kept it, didn’t it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power? How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven’t lied to men, but to God.”

lessons.title: Overflowing in Thanks to God
lessons.hear:
This week we started from grace and learned to give cheerfully. At the end of this passage, Paul widens the lens: the effect of giving is not only that it “makes up for lack among the saints, but abounds also through much giving of thanks to God” (2 Corinthians 9:12).

Giving is like a river. It flows out of God’s grace, passes through our hands, reaches the needs of the body, and finally turns into thanks and praise flowing back to God. The believers in Jerusalem who received help would, Paul says, “with supplication on your behalf, yearn for you” (2 Corinthians 9:14). The movement of money actually became a bridge of unity between Jewish and Gentile believers.

The Old Testament has a beautiful scene of this. When the tabernacle was being built, “everyone whose heart stirred him up, and everyone whom his spirit made willing, … brought the LORD’s offering” (Exodus 35:21)—so much that Moses had to tell the people to stop (see Exodus 36:5-7). When God’s people are touched by grace, the building lacks nothing.

Multiplication means passing this gladness on. Not by persuading others how much to give, but by sharing stories of grace: how you moved from grudging to glad, and where you experienced God’s faithfulness. You can begin at home, too. Let your child put a bit of their own pocket money into the offering on Sunday, and tell them, “We’re not paying God; we’re thanking God.”

Finally, let us say with Paul: “Now thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift!” (2 Corinthians 9:15). The source of all our giving is that God first gave us his Son.
lessons.light: The final step in changing a mindset is multiplication. If the grace of giving stops with me, I become a Dead Sea; only when it flows out does it become living water. Let Jesus receive all the glory—not so that my generosity is praised, but so that many overflow in thanks to God.
think: In 2 Corinthians 9:12-15, what spiritual fruit did the giving produce?
How has my view of giving changed this week?
With whom will I share the grace I have experienced in giving, and when?
lessons.speak: Thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift! Thank you for renewing my view of giving this week. Make our church a river of grace—flowing from you, passing through us, blessing the body, and finally returning to you as thanksgiving. Help me pass this gladness on to my family and companions. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, find your spiritual companion or a family member and spend five minutes sharing a story of experiencing God’s provision or learning to give gladly. Leave out the amounts and talk only about grace; then pray together for the needs of the church.
lessons.quick: Flowing out from grace, flowing back as thanks: that is cheerful giving.
text: For this service of giving that you perform not only makes up for lack among the saints, but abounds also through much giving of thanks to God,
seeing that through the proof given by this service, they glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the Good News of Christ and for the generosity of your contribution to them and to all,
while they themselves also, with supplication on your behalf, yearn for you by reason of the exceeding grace of God in you.
Now thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift!

weeks.title: Offering Our Time, Talents, and Gifts
weeks.keyText: redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
weeks.theme: Our time, talents, and gifts are all entrusted to us by the Lord; redeem the time and use what you have received to build up the body of Christ.
group: Read Ephesians 5:15-21. What does “redeeming the time” mean in your current situation?
What most often “buries” or “takes captive” your time or your gifts?
Which block of time or which talent are you willing to offer concretely to your small group or to one member of the body this week?
weeks.sunday: This Lord’s Day, arrive or log on ten minutes early and give those ten minutes to the Lord: pray for the service and welcome one newcomer. During the service, notice who is quietly serving; afterward, thank one of them, and ask yourself: What talent does the Lord want me to bring into this body?

lessons.title: Buying Back the Time
lessons.hear:
We often say, “I don’t have time.” Work, family, commuting, our phones—twenty-four hours never seem to be enough. Yet Paul reminds us to be “redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:16). The word “redeem” carries the sense of buying back, paying to set free. Our time is like a captive, snatched away by all kinds of things; Christians are to use wisdom to buy it back and hand it over for the Lord’s use.

Paul sets redeeming the time within a series of contrasts: not unwise, but wise; not foolish, but understanding the Lord’s will; not drunk with wine, but filled with the Spirit. Redeeming the time does not mean cramming our calendar even fuller. It means first understanding “what the will of the Lord is” (Ephesians 5:17), and then letting the Holy Spirit arrange our time.

Interestingly, what Paul says next is not “work harder” but church life: “speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19), giving thanks for all things and submitting to one another. A large share of our redeemed time is meant to be invested in God and in God’s household.

In the wilderness Moses prayed, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). Counting our days means admitting that our time is limited, and admitting that it belongs to God. Giving is not only money; it is also time: an evening spent with a new believer, a morning teaching a Sunday school class, ten minutes praying for a brother or sister.

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on your day. Which hours have been taken captive? Which can be bought back and offered to the Lord and his body?
lessons.light: The self-centered person says, “my time”; the selfless person says, “the time the Lord has entrusted to me.” From a temporary point of view, time is for building up myself; from an eternal point of view, time is for building God’s system. Arranging my time with my heart, relying on the Holy Spirit, is wiser than planning it with my head, relying on myself.
think: In Ephesians 5:15-21, what contrasts does Paul use to describe the wise person?
What most often takes my time captive?
Which block of time can I buy back this week and offer to the Lord or to a brother or sister?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I often say I have no time, yet I spend so much of it on things that don’t profit. Teach me to count my days so that I may gain a heart of wisdom. Holy Spirit, fill me and lead my calendar, so that I buy back the time that has been taken captive and give it to you and to your body. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, review how you spent today and identify a block of time taken captive by your phone or by trivial things (say, thirty minutes). Tomorrow, buy it back: use it to pray and read Scripture, or to send a message checking in on a brother or sister.
lessons.quick: Time isn’t mine; it’s entrusted by the Lord. Buy back the time that’s been taken captive.
text: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise,
redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Therefore, don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit,
speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father;
subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.

lessons.title: Don’t Bury Your Talent
lessons.hear:
For seven years one brother sat in the pews and always said he had “no gifts.” He couldn’t sing, couldn’t preach, wasn’t good at leading a small group—all he knew was fixing computers. Then one year the church suddenly had to move its services online, and everyone was scrambling. He quietly set up the equipment and taught the older members, one by one, how to log on—and he kept at it for months. Later he shared in his small group: “I used to think only what happens up front counted as serving. It turns out the Lord put something in my hands long ago; I had just buried it.”

The Lord Jesus told a parable. A master gave his servants money, “to each according to his own ability” (Matthew 25:15). The amounts differed, but every one of them received something. The servants with five talents and two talents went straight off to trade; but the one with one talent “went away and dug in the earth, and hid his lord’s money” (Matthew 25:18).

Why did he bury it? He told us himself: “Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man … I was afraid” (Matthew 25:24-25). The root of the problem was not that his ability was too small, but that his picture of his master was wrong. He thought his master was harsh, so all he wanted was to protect himself and avoid mistakes.

The old mindsets we tend to carry sound like this: “My gift is too small to matter.” “I’ll serve once I retire, once the kids are grown.” “If I do it badly I’ll be criticized, so better not to do it at all.” But God’s view is that every member of the body has received a trust from the Lord, and what the Lord looks at is not the size of the amount but faithfulness. The servant with two talents received word-for-word the same praise as the one with five: “Well done, good and faithful servant.”

The one talent in your hand may be cooking, organizing, driving, bookkeeping, design, or the patience to walk alongside people. It isn’t yours; it is the Lord’s. Dig it up! The Lord is good, and he will not look down on you because your gift is small.
lessons.light: Burying our gifts can look like humility, but it is often self-centeredness: fear of failure, fear of embarrassment, fear of not measuring up to others—every focus is on self. The selfless person’s focus is on Jesus: he entrusts, so I am faithful; success and failure are in the Lord’s hands, and so is the glory.
think: In Matthew 25:14-25, why did the servant with one talent bury it?
Does my picture of God make me fearful and hold me back from serving?
What “one talent” do I have in my hands that I can dig up and use?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that I often bury the gifts you have given me, thinking they are too small or too ordinary, or afraid I’ll do badly. Renew my picture of you: you are a good Lord. Give me courage to bring out the talents you have put in my hands and to use them faithfully in your body. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down three things you can do, enjoy doing, and have helped others with. Pick one and ask a co-worker or small group leader, “Where could the church use this?”
lessons.quick: The Lord isn’t asking how much you were given, but whether you buried it.
text: “For it is like a man going into another country, who called his own servants and entrusted his goods to them.
To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his own ability. Then he went on his journey.
Immediately he who received the five talents went and traded with them, and made another five talents.
In the same way, he also who got the two gained another two.
But he who received the one talent went away and dug in the earth and hid his lord’s money.
“Now after a long time the lord of those servants came, and settled accounts with them.
He who received the five talents came and brought another five talents, saying, ‘Lord, you delivered to me five talents. Behold, I have gained another five talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
“He also who got the two talents came and said, ‘Lord, you delivered to me two talents. Behold, I have gained another two talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things. I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
“He also who had received the one talent came and said, ‘Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man, reaping where you didn’t sow, and gathering where you didn’t scatter.
I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.’

lessons.title: Serving with the Gifts We’ve Received
lessons.hear:
Paul writes that we have “gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us” (Romans 12:6). He goes on to list prophecy, service, teaching, exhorting, giving, leading, and showing mercy—some up front and some behind the scenes, some with the mouth, some with the hands, and more with the heart. Different gifts fit together to form a healthy body.

Gifts aren’t only “spiritual” abilities, either. In the Old Testament, Bezalel, who built the tabernacle, was a craftsman, and God said, “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship” (Exodus 31:3). Carving, setting stones, spinning, embroidery—in God’s eyes, all of it can be the work of the Spirit. Your profession, skills, and life experience, once placed in the Lord’s hands, become building materials.

Notice the way Paul describes how each gift is to be used: service, give yourself to it; the one who gives, “with generosity”; the one who leads, “with diligence”; the one who shows mercy, “with cheerfulness” (Romans 12:7-8). The quality of our service is not about scale but about the attitude of the heart. He sums it up: “not lagging in diligence; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord” (Romans 12:11).

Today’s practice is very concrete: give a block of time or one of your talents to a real person or a specific need. Perhaps you can watch a single mom’s children for two hours so she can get to a meeting; perhaps help an older brother sort out his paperwork; perhaps sign up for next month’s welcome team or children’s ministry rotation. You don’t have to take on too much at once. Take one small step first, and tell the person in charge clearly how much you can do and for how long.

When you do this, you aren’t just “helping out.” You are serving “as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms” (1 Peter 4:10).
lessons.light: The Way of Service begins with “Spirit”: the Holy Spirit is my guide. It isn’t gritting my teeth to fill whatever gap appears, nor choosing only what I like; it is asking the Lord in prayer, “Where do you want me to fit in?” When Jesus reigns, our talents become gifts; when self reigns, even our gifts can turn into pride.
think: What attitudes does Romans 12:6-11 pair with the different gifts?
How could my profession or life experience become building material for the church?
Which block of time or which talent will I offer today, and to whom?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for distributing gifts to every member of the body through the Holy Spirit—including me. Help me see what I have received, without envying others or looking down on myself. Lead me today to give my time and talents to someone in need, and to serve wholeheartedly, generously, diligently, and cheerfully. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, reach out to a brother, sister, or co-worker and make a specific offer of your time or talent—for example, “I can give you two hours on Saturday afternoon to help with …”—and set a time to do it.
lessons.quick: My talent, placed in the Lord’s hands, becomes a gift that builds the body.
text: having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith;
or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching;
or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.
Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.
In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,
not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,

lessons.title: Martha, Distracted
lessons.hear:
Martha was a woman with tremendous zeal for serving. When Jesus came to her village, she was the one who “received him into her house” (Luke 10:38). But before long she “was distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40). She began to resent her sister, and even complained to Jesus: “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone?”

This is a portrait of many devoted ministry team members. It starts out being for the Lord; then, without our noticing, it becomes about getting things done, getting them done well, doing more than everyone else. The more we serve, the wearier our hearts become, and the more irritated we are with those who aren’t serving. The Lord says gently, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed” (Luke 10:41-42).

When it comes to offering our time and talents, there are two common errors. One is “burying,” which we looked at in an earlier lesson. The other is “overdrawing”: giving all our time to church ministry while neglecting intimacy with the Lord, our own body and soul, and the needs of our family. Some people are the most dependable person at the ministry team meeting yet are absent parents at home. That is not the offering God wants. God wants us first to sit at his feet and receive, and then to rise and serve; he also wants us to honor rest and be faithful within our limits.

Today, review honestly: Am I “distracted” in my serving? Has comparison bred bitterness in me? Do I find it hard to say “no”? Adjusting doesn’t mean quitting ministry; it means putting things back in order: first God, then myself, then people, then tasks.

What became of Martha? After Lazarus died, it was Martha who made that moving confession: “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son” (John 11:27). A distracted servant can also become someone who knows the Lord deeply.
lessons.light: People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. Don’t hurt people for the sake of a task, and don’t hurt yourself or your family for it either. Self-centered service is trying to prove itself, so it can’t stop; selfless service knows the Lord is Lord, so it can rest. Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart and you’ll find joy; rely on yourself with your head and you’ll find worry.
think: In Luke 10:38-42, what is the difference between Martha and Mary?
In my serving, do I lean toward burying, overdrawing, or first receiving at the Lord’s feet?
What one thing do I need to adjust this week to get back to the right order?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I am often like Martha, anxious and troubled about many things, even resenting the people around me. Forgive me for putting serving ahead of you. Today I choose to sit at your feet first and receive your love again. Help me live in the right order, to be faithful within my limits and to serve from a place of rest. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, list all your current ministries and commitments, and before the Lord mark the one that leaves you most “distracted.” If something needs adjusting, take the initiative this week to talk with the person in charge and be honest about your limits.
lessons.quick: Only one thing is needed: sit at the Lord’s feet first, then rise to serve.
text: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.title: A Heart to Teach Others
lessons.hear:
This week we have seen that our time, talents, and gifts are all entrusted to us by the Lord. Today let’s go back to the building of the tabernacle and watch how God lets gifts multiply.

Bezalel was a craftsman whom God called by name and filled with his Spirit. But the passage goes on: “He has put in his heart that he may teach, both he and Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan” (Exodus 35:34). God gave them not only skill but a heart to teach others. The tabernacle was not finished by two lone geniuses; it was built by a whole company of men and women with wisdom in their hearts.

Here is the principle of multiplying gifts: a good steward not only does the work well but hands on what he knows to others. Paul told Timothy, “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). In one short sentence there are four generations of handing on.

Think about how many ministries in the church get stuck because “only so-and-so knows how”: only one brother can run the sound desk, only one sister can play the piano, only one deacon understands the books. When that person gets tired, moves away, or falls ill, the ministry grinds to a halt. That is not the finish line of faithfulness; it means the handing on is not yet complete. The best kind of serving makes yourself replaceable.

This week, invite a young person or a newcomer to serve alongside you once. Teach as you go, so that they see, learn, and taste the joy of serving. When gifts are passed on, the Lord’s house is built up from generation to generation.
lessons.light: This is where the 235 practice becomes real: partnering with selfless companions (2), passing on what we have learned to spiritual children (3), and becoming a team that builds together (5). The self-centered person is afraid of being replaced; the selfless person is glad to be surpassed. Let Jesus receive the glory, rather than making myself indispensable.
think: In Exodus 35:30-35, besides craftsmanship, what else did God give Bezalel?
Is there anything in my ministry that “only I know how to do”?
Whom can I invite to serve with me this week, so I can teach them what I know?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for entrusting me with time, talents, and gifts. Give me, too, a heart to teach others—unafraid of being replaced and glad to see others grow. Lead me to the person who can serve alongside me, so that your house is built from generation to generation and you receive all the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a newcomer, a young person, or a small group member to join you the next time you serve. Afterward, spend ten minutes sharing why you serve, and pray for them.
lessons.quick: A good steward doesn’t just do the work, but hands it on to the next person.
text: Moses said to the children of Israel, “Behold, the LORD has called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah.
He has filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, in understanding, in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship;
and to make skillful works, to work in gold, in silver, in bronze,
in cutting of stones for setting, and in carving of wood, to work in all kinds of skillful workmanship.
He has put in his heart that he may teach, both he and Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan.

He has filled them with wisdom of heart to work all kinds of workmanship, of the engraver, of the skillful workman, and of the embroiderer, in blue, in purple, in scarlet, and in fine linen, and of the weaver, even of those who do any workmanship, and of those who make skillful works.

weeks.title: Praying with One Accord
weeks.keyText: All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.
weeks.theme: Prayer is the church’s breath; praying with one accord opens the door for the Holy Spirit to move in the church.
group: Read Acts 1:12-14. What did the disciples do while they waited for the Holy Spirit? Who was there?
What are your feelings about, or experiences of, your church’s prayer meetings? Why do you think that is?
Which brother or sister will you arrange to pray with in one accord this week? When and how?
weeks.sunday: This Lord’s Day, arrive or log on early and spend five minutes praying for the service, the speaker, and any newcomers. When someone leads in prayer during the service, don’t just listen—say “amen” in your heart and join them in one accord. Afterward, invite a brother or sister to pray with you for one minute about one need in the church.

lessons.title: One Accord in the Upper Room
lessons.hear:
Before he ascended, the Lord Jesus told his disciples to “wait in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). How did they wait? Not by holding a meeting to draft a strategy, and not by going home to rest. They gathered in an upper room: “All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication, along with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers” (Acts 1:14).

Look at that list of names. There was Peter, who had denied the Lord three times; Thomas, who had doubted; Matthew, the former tax collector; and Simon the Zealot—one man who had collected taxes for Rome and another who had resisted Rome. There were several women, and Jesus’ own brothers, who earlier had not believed in him (see John 7:5). Humanly speaking, these were people of different backgrounds, personalities, and politics; yet in prayer they were of one accord.

“With one accord” is a phrase that keeps reappearing in Acts, running like a red thread through the early church. A few days later, “when the day of Pentecost had come, they were all with one accord in one place” (Acts 2:1), and the Holy Spirit came down. The church was born in a prayer meeting.

Prayer is the church’s breath. A person can go days without food but not minutes without breathing; a church can run far fewer programs, but it cannot go without prayer. In the Old Testament, God promised: “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven” (2 Chronicles 7:14).

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to help you see that the church’s power does not come from human plans but from praying with one accord.
lessons.light: Being of one accord requires selflessness. If we bring our own positions, our pride, and our agendas into prayer, we will only talk past one another. When we lay ourselves down and let Jesus reign, very different people can become one before the same Lord. Prayer itself is humility: admitting it does not depend on me but on God.
think: In Acts 1:12-14, who was praying with one accord? How were they different from one another?
Do I rely more on the church’s plans or on prayer?
How can I take part in my church’s united prayer this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for making disciples of such different backgrounds one in prayer. Make our church a house of prayer, too, relying not on human plans but on your Spirit. Forgive me for so often leaving prayer until last. Today I choose to be of one accord with my brothers and sisters and to wait for your power. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find out what prayer gatherings your church or small group holds (in person or online). Choose one you will attend this month, put it in your calendar, and invite a brother or sister to go with you.
lessons.quick: The church was born in prayer, and it breathes by prayer.
text: Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away.

When they had come in, they went up into the upper room where they were staying, that is Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James.
All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.

lessons.title: The Promise for Two or Three
lessons.hear:
At one church, the midweek prayer meeting was usually just five or six older members. The young people thought of it as “the seniors’ meeting” and figured praying on their own was enough. Then a brother from one of the small groups went through a stretch of intense pressure at work, and he finally worked up the courage to go once. There was no lively worship that night and no inspiring sharing. A few older ladies simply knelt together and prayed, one after another, for the church, for the sick, and for the young people’s jobs. When it ended, an elderly sister took his hand and said, “Every week we pray for you young people.” His eyes filled with tears. All along, without his knowing, someone had been keeping watch over him.

The old mindsets we often carry sound like this: “Prayer is private; praying on my own is enough.” “Prayer meetings are small and dull; I’d be better off doing something practical.” But the Lord Jesus said, “if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:19).

The word translated “agree” shares its root with our word “symphony”—sounding together in harmony. A violin can play solo, but a symphony needs different instruments playing together under one conductor. Personal prayer is precious, but praying in agreement carries a special promise: “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them” (Matthew 18:20).

This doesn’t mean that enough people can force God’s hand. It means that when members of the body lay aside their own opinions and seek the Lord’s will together, the Lord himself is there among them. The psalmist says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1). Praying in one accord is the church’s most beautiful harmony.
lessons.light: The self-centered person says, “I’ll just pray on my own.” It sounds spiritual, but it may really be an unwillingness to share the yoke with others. The selfless person is willing to be of one accord with fellow members, knowing the body of Christ needs one another. People matter more than events: a prayer meeting is not a program but a group of members coming together before the Head.
think: In Matthew 18:19-20, what two promises does the Lord Jesus make about praying together?
Do I often substitute “I’ll just pray on my own” for praying with others?
Whom could I ask to become a regular prayer partner?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for promising to be with us wherever two or three gather in the Lord’s name. I confess I have often looked down on praying together, thinking my own prayers were enough. Make me humble and willing to be of one accord with my brothers and sisters, so that together we make harmony before you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact a spiritual companion or a small group member and set a time this week to pray together for fifteen minutes, by phone or in person. Each share one need and pray for each other.
lessons.quick: Where two or three agree in prayer, the Lord is there among them.
text: Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.”

lessons.title: Lifting Our Voices Together Under Threat
lessons.hear:
After Peter and John were threatened by the council and released, the first thing they did was go “to their own company” (Acts 4:23). When the church heard the news, they didn’t call a meeting to plan countermeasures, and they didn’t blame one another. Instead, “they lifted up their voice to God with one accord” (Acts 4:24). Their prayer is a beautiful model of praying together, and it follows three steps.

First, they looked up to who God is: “O Lord, you are God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them” (Acts 4:24). When the problem is big, first fix your eyes on the bigger God. Second, they prayed God’s word. They quoted Psalm 2: “Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing?” (Psalm 2:1), and saw that the persecution in front of them had long been within God’s plan. Third, they asked for God’s will to be done. They didn’t ask God to remove the persecution; they asked him to “grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness” (Acts 4:29). The result: “When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness” (Acts 4:31).

Today’s practice is to use these three steps to pray with one real brother or sister. Find someone who is facing a hardship—perhaps trouble at work, a sick family member, or a rebellious child—and ask for ten minutes, by phone or in person. First praise God together for who he is, then read a fitting verse, and finally ask together, “Lord, in this matter, may your will be done.”

You don’t have to pray long or fluently. The power of praying together is not in eloquent words but in looking up together to the Lord who made heaven and earth.
lessons.light: Keep your focus on Jesus—not on yourself, not on others, not on circumstances. Under threat, the early church didn’t look at their circumstances; they looked to the Lord who made heaven and earth. A prayer that lets Jesus reign doesn’t ask God to change circumstances to suit me; it asks God to make us bold witnesses in the middle of them.
think: In the prayer of Acts 4:23-31, how did the disciples address God? What did they ask for?
When trouble comes, is my first reaction to find someone to complain to, or someone to pray with?
Which brother or sister will I pray with today using these three steps?
lessons.speak: Lord, who made the heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, you are the God who reigns. Help me in hardship to look up to you first, to pray your word, and to ask for your will to be done. Lead me today to pray in one accord with a brother or sister, so that we are not intimidated by our circumstances but filled with the Holy Spirit and bold to witness for you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, arrange ten minutes to pray with a brother or sister facing a hardship: first praise God, then read a verse, and finally ask together for God’s will to be done. Write down what you prayed for, and check in with them again in a week.
lessons.quick: First look up to God, then pray his word, and finally ask for his will.
text: Being let go, they came to their own company and reported all that the chief priests and the elders had said to them.
When they heard it, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord and said, “O Lord, you are God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them;
who by the mouth of your servant David, said, ‘Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing?
The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers plot together, against the Lord, and against his Christ.’
“For truly, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed,
to do whatever your hand and your counsel foreordained to happen.
Now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness,
while you stretch out your hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus.”
When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness.

lessons.title: Praying, but Not Believing
lessons.hear:
Peter had been imprisoned by Herod, “but constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him” (Acts 12:5). And God did send an angel to rescue him. Peter came and knocked at the door of the house where people had gathered to pray. A servant girl named Rhoda recognized his voice and was so overjoyed that she forgot to open the gate and ran inside to tell everyone. But the very people who were praying for Peter said to her, “You are crazy!” (Acts 12:15).

The scene is a little comical—and very true to life. They were praying earnestly, yet they didn’t really expect God to answer. Peter kept knocking outside, and they couldn’t bring themselves to believe it inside. God’s answer was already standing at the door.

This mirror reveals several blind spots in our prayer life. First, prayer becomes routine: we say the words and forget them, expecting nothing. Second, prayer requests turn into news swapping, even a disguised form of gossip: “Did you hear what’s going on in so-and-so’s family?” Third, prayer turns into a disguised sermon or a venting session, dressing up our complaints about others as prayer for everyone to hear. Fourth, we look united on the surface while there is distance in our hearts. The Lord Jesus said that if you remember your brother has something against you, “leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24). Prayer is the same.

The way of adjustment is not complicated. Before praying, deal with your relationships with others. While praying, expect in faith. After praying, watch for God’s answer, and guard your fellow members’ privacy.

Here is the comfort: even though their faith was small, God still answered. God’s faithfulness does not rest on our perfection. Today, bring your little faith to the Lord; he is still willing to open the door.
lessons.light: Self-centered prayer revolves around me: speaking for others to hear, saving face, turning other people’s troubles into topics of conversation. Selfless prayer revolves around God: coming humbly and waiting trustingly. Pride stirs up pride, and humility draws out humility; the atmosphere of a prayer meeting begins to change in my own heart.
think: In Acts 12:12-17, how did the people who were praying react when they heard Peter had come?
Is there anything in my praying that is expectationless, gossipy, or performative?
Before the next prayer gathering I attend, what one thing will I adjust first?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that I often pray without expecting anything, and that I have even treated prayer requests as topics for talk. Forgive my little faith and my careless tongue. Cleanse my heart so that I am reconciled with others before I come to you, and help me wait in faith to see your answer at the door. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Recall something you once prayed for that God answered, but you forgot to give thanks. Today, thank God for it specifically. If you have ever let someone’s private matters slip while sharing prayer requests, confess it to the Lord and learn to guard their confidence.
lessons.quick: After you pray, remember to open the door—God’s answer is often already outside.
text: Thinking about that, he came to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
When Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer.
When she recognized Peter’s voice, she didn’t open the gate for joy, but ran in and reported that Peter was standing in front of the gate.
They said to her, “You are crazy!” But she insisted that it was so. They said, “It is his angel.”
But Peter continued knocking. When they had opened, they saw him and were amazed.

But he, beckoning to them with his hand to be silent, declared to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. He said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place.

lessons.title: Even the Little Ones Stood There
lessons.hear:
When King Jehoshaphat of Judah faced a vast army bearing down on him, his first reaction was this: “Jehoshaphat was alarmed, and set himself to seek the LORD. He proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah.” (2 Chronicles 20:3). The king did not first deploy his troops; he called the whole nation together to pray.

His prayer was utterly honest: “For we have no might against this great company that comes against us. We don’t know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (2 Chronicles 20:12). The deepest place in praying together is a group of people admitting together, “We don’t know, but we look to you.”

Then comes a verse that is easy to overlook: “All Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children” (2 Chronicles 20:13). That day’s prayer meeting was not just for the adults. The children were there too, watching with their own eyes how their parents looked to God in a crisis.

This is how prayer multiplies. A church’s tradition of prayer is not built by one special conference; it is handed down through spiritual families, generation after generation. When children see Mom and Dad praying together before dinner, when they see their small group holding hands and calling on God in hard times, they learn: when something happens, go to God first.

This week we have seen the prayer in the upper room, the promise to two or three, boldness under threat, and grace in the midst of little faith. Now pass it on. Bring a newcomer to a prayer meeting for the first time, teach a new believer to pray in simple words, or start a weekly family prayer time at home. Let praying with one accord become the breath that the church hands down from generation to generation.
lessons.light: The final step in changing a mindset is multiplication. If prayer is only my personal discipline, it stops with my generation; if I pray together with the next generation and with newcomers, it becomes the foundation of God’s system. May God’s kingdom come, beginning with one household after another that prays in one accord.
think: In 2 Chronicles 20:3-13, how did Jehoshaphat and the people face the crisis? Who else was there?
How has my view of praying together changed this week?
Whom will I bring along to pray with me, to pass this practice on?
lessons.speak: Father, so often we don’t know what to do, but our eyes are on you. Thank you for teaching me this week to pray in one accord. Make my home, my small group, and our church houses of prayer, and let the next generation come to know your faithfulness through our prayers. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, choose an evening to pray for ten minutes with your family, roommates, or small group members. If possible, invite a new believer or a child to pray one sentence, and say “amen” to their prayer.
lessons.quick: We don’t know what to do, but our eyes are on the Lord.
text: Jehoshaphat was alarmed, and set himself to seek the LORD. He proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah.
Judah gathered themselves together to seek help from the LORD. They came out of all the cities of Judah to seek the LORD.
Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem, in the LORD’s house, before the new court;
and he said, “LORD, the God of our fathers, aren’t you God in heaven? Aren’t you ruler over all the kingdoms of the nations? Power and might are in your hand, so that no one is able to withstand you.
Didn’t you, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it to the offspring of Abraham your friend forever?
They lived in it, and have built you a sanctuary in it for your name, saying,

‘If evil comes on us—the sword, judgment, pestilence, or famine—we will stand before this house, and before you (for your name is in this house), and cry to you in our affliction, and you will hear and save.’
Now, behold, the children of Ammon and Moab and Mount Seir, whom you would not let Israel invade when they came out of the land of Egypt, but they turned away from them, and didn’t destroy them;
behold, how they reward us, to come to cast us out of your possession, which you have given us to inherit.
Our God, will you not judge them? For we have no might against this great company that comes against us. We don’t know what to do, but our eyes are on you.”
All Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children.

weeks.title: Keeping Watch in Prayer for One Another
weeks.keyText: Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.
weeks.theme: Intercession is the most hidden and the most powerful kind of love; in prayer we keep watch over our pastors, our fellow members, and our city.
group: Read James 5:13-18. What situations does James say call for prayer? Where does “one another” appear?
Has someone’s prayer for you ever been a special help to you? Share that experience.
This week, have each person in the small group choose one fellow member and one pastor or ministry team member, and agree with one another to pray for them every day. Who will you choose?
weeks.sunday: This Lord’s Day, bring a small slip of paper to the service with three names on it: a pastor or ministry team member, a brother or sister in the church, and a friend or relative who doesn’t yet believe. During the service, quietly pray for the one preaching. Afterward, ask a brother or sister, “What can I pray for you this week?” and write it down.

lessons.title: Praying for One Another, Being Healed
lessons.hear:
At the end of his letter, James gives a string of very down-to-earth instructions: “Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praises” (James 5:13). Suffering, joy, sickness, sin—every situation in life can and should be brought into prayer. And we don’t bring them alone; we bring them together, in the church.

James says, “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.” (James 5:16). There are two “one anothers” here: confess to one another, and pray for one another. Intercession is built on open, trusting relationships; only a place where it is safe to name our weaknesses can be a place where we pray for one another. And the healing in view is not only physical; it includes the healing of relationships and of the soul.

Perhaps you think, “A ‘righteous person’—that’s a long way from me.” James immediately gives Elijah as an example: “Elijah was a man with a nature like ours” (James 5:17). He too got discouraged and afraid; he even asked to die in the wilderness. Yet on the top of Mount Carmel “he bowed himself down on the earth, and put his face between his knees” (1 Kings 18:42), and sent his servant to look again and again, until the seventh time he saw a small cloud rising from the sea. The power of intercession lies not in how spiritual we are but in the God we call upon.

Intercession is the most hidden way of loving one another. No one sees it, no one praises it, and sometimes even the person we pray for never knows. But in heaven, every name spoken for a brother or sister is remembered by the God who hears prayer. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to lay one or two names on your heart.
lessons.light: Intercession is the most direct practice of 920: everyone connected to me is my “2,” and I can bring them before the Lord every day. The self-centered person prays only about their own needs; the selfless person carries other people’s burdens on their heart—and this is the life of Christ being lived out in me.
think: In James 5:13-18, what situations call for prayer?
Do I have a relationship in which we can confess to one another and pray for one another?
Which one or two names is the Holy Spirit laying on my heart today?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for hearing prayer. Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, yet you heard his prayer. Make me someone who keeps watch in prayer for my brothers and sisters, and give me one or two companions with whom I can confess and pray for one another. Today I place in your hands the names you have laid on my heart. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the names of two brothers or sisters the Holy Spirit has laid on your heart, and pray for each of them for three minutes. Then send each a short message: “I prayed for you today. Is there anything in particular you need?”
lessons.quick: Intercession is the most hidden love, and the most powerful.
text: Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praises.
Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the assembly, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord;
and the prayer of faith will heal him who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. If he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.
Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it didn’t rain on the earth for three years and six months.
He prayed again, and the sky gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit.

lessons.title: Epaphras, Striving in Prayer
lessons.hear:
We often hear people say, “There’s nothing I can do to help—all I can do is pray for you.” As if intercession were a consolation prize, handed out once every other option has run out.

One sister in her eighties, unsteady on her feet, had not been able to get to church for a long time and often felt she was “no use anymore.” Then her small group leader began sending her the weekly prayer list. Every morning she went down the list, praying one by one for the brothers and sisters, the pastors, and the young people. A few years later she went home to be with the Lord, and only at her memorial service did many people learn that, all through those years, they had been remembered by a sister they never saw. One ministry team member said, “If our church made it through those hard years, it was on her knees.”

In Colossians, Paul mentions a not-very-prominent co-worker named Epaphras, who was “always striving for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God” (Colossians 4:12). The word “striving” carries the sense of wrestling with all one’s might; it comes from the same root as an athlete’s contest in the arena. Paul also testifies that Epaphras “has great zeal for you” (Colossians 4:13). Intercession is not a light word of blessing; it is spiritual labor.

In the Old Testament, Samuel even said, “Moreover as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you” (1 Samuel 12:23). For Samuel, failing to pray for the people was actually a sin.

So intercession is not “all I can do”; it is “look what I get to do”: through prayer, we actually get to take part in God’s work in someone else’s life. This is a privilege God gives every member of the body—young or old, strong or frail.
lessons.light: Change your viewpoint and you change your mindset. From a human point of view, intercession is the fallback when we can’t help; from God’s point of view, it is front-line ministry. Proud people feel that only what they do themselves counts; humble people know that everything is accomplished by God—which is why the humble understand intercession best.
think: In Colossians 4:2-4, 12, what does Paul ask people to pray for him? And how does Epaphras pray?
Have I ever regarded intercession as a small thing, “all I can do”?
How can I learn from Epaphras to strive in prayer for my brothers and sisters?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, forgive me for so often treating intercession as a last resort. Thank you that through prayer I actually get to take part in your work. Give me the heart of Epaphras, to strive in prayer for my brothers and sisters, that they may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose one brother or sister and, following Colossians 4:12, pray three specific things for them: that they stand firm, that they grow to maturity, and that they be fully assured in all the will of God. Write them down and keep praying for this person tomorrow.
lessons.quick: Intercession isn’t “all I can do”—it’s the privilege of sharing in God’s work.
text: Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving,
praying together for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds,
that I may reveal it as I ought to speak.
Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, salutes you, always striving for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.

lessons.title: For All the Saints—and for Our Pastors
lessons.hear:
Paul describes the whole armor of God, and his final word is not another weapon but prayer: “with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints” (Ephesians 6:18). Intercessors are like watchmen on the city wall, guarding the places where our brothers and sisters are most vulnerable to attack.

Then Paul says, “for me, that utterance may be given to me in opening my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the Good News” (Ephesians 6:19). This great apostle openly asked believers to pray for him; he was not afraid to admit he had needs. The same is true of pastors, preachers, and ministry team members. They stand on the front lines, facing more pressure, temptation, and attack than we often imagine, yet few people ever ask them, “How can I pray for you?”

The prophet Isaiah describes God setting watchmen over Jerusalem: “I have set watchmen on your walls, Jerusalem. They will never be silent day nor night” (Isaiah 62:6). Today, God wants to set watchmen in the church too.

Today’s practice is to build your own watch list. It doesn’t have to be long, and it can have three tiers. Tier one: one or two pastors or ministry team members. Tier two: three to five people from your small group or those close to you in the church. Tier three: one or two friends or relatives who don’t yet know the Lord. Each day, choose one tier to pray for. For pastors, ask for wisdom, protection for their families, and power in their preaching; for fellow members, ask for strengthened faith and provision for their needs; for friends and relatives, ask that the eyes of their hearts be opened.

Then pick one pastor or ministry team member and send them a message today: “What can I pray for you this week?” You may never know that this one sentence could be their greatest comfort all week.
lessons.light: The relationships of 235 are built in prayer: keeping watch for each other with our companions (2), interceding for our spiritual parents and children (3), and holding up the arms of those serving in the five-fold ministry (5). Not criticizing our pastors behind their backs, but praying for them behind the scenes—this is the culture of a church where Jesus reigns.
think: In Ephesians 6:18-20, what does Paul ask others to pray for him?
When did I last pray specifically for my pastor or a ministry team member?
What names will I put in each of the three tiers of my watch list?
lessons.speak: Father, make me a watchman who stays alert and does not grow weary. I bring before you my pastors, my ministry team members, the brothers and sisters around me, and my friends and family who don’t yet believe. Guard their hearts and minds and their families, and give them wisdom and strength. And make me someone who prays for people behind their backs rather than talking about them behind their backs. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write out your three-tier watch list, and send a message to a pastor or ministry team member: “What can I pray for you this week?” When they reply, pray for them that same day.
lessons.quick: Don’t talk about people behind their backs—pray for them behind the scenes.
text: with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints.
Pray for me, that utterance may be given to me in opening my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the Good News,
for which I am an ambassador in chains; that in it I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.

lessons.title: “I Prayed for You”
lessons.hear:
On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus said to Peter, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat, but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail” (Luke 22:31-32). The Lord already knew Peter would deny him three times, but instead of rebuking him first, he prayed for him first. He did not pray that Peter would never fall, but that after falling his faith would not fail—and “You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

This is the highest example of intercession, and it is also today’s mirror for review. When I learn that a brother or sister is struggling, has fallen, or is caught up in a controversy, what is my first reaction? To dig for details, pass it on, and comment—or to pray for them first? Sometimes we say, “Please pray for so-and-so,” when we are really spreading someone’s private business. True intercession guards the tongue and protects the dignity of fellow members.

Harder still is praying for those who have hurt us. Job’s friends wounded him with many self-righteous words, yet in the end God told Job to pray for them. Scripture says, “The LORD restored Job’s prosperity when he prayed for his friends” (Job 42:10). Praying for someone who has hurt you does not mean pretending you weren’t hurt, nor does it mean instantly restoring trust. Prayer hands judgment over to God and lets my own heart go free first. If the harm involves spiritual abuse or any form of mistreatment, please also seek help from a trusted pastor or a professional; intercession does not replace protection or getting help.

Peter really did turn back, and he went on to strengthen many brothers. And the Lord who prayed for Peter still “lives forever to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25)—and he is interceding for you right now.
lessons.light: When someone else falls, the self-centered person thinks, “I knew it all along”; the selfless person thinks, “Lord, please keep their faith from failing.” A proud tongue spreads weakness; humble knees cover it. Letting Jesus reign means looking at a fallen brother or sister with his heart.
think: In Luke 22:31-34, what did the Lord Jesus pray for Peter?
When I hear about a fellow member’s weakness, do I talk about it first or pray first?
Is there someone who has hurt me whom I am willing to begin praying for?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you that you live forever to intercede for me. I confess that I often make other people’s weaknesses a topic of conversation instead of praying for them. Cleanse my tongue, and make me like you—praying first, then speaking. Give me strength, too, to pray for those who have hurt me, handing judgment over to you so that my heart can be free. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of the last time you passed on a fellow member’s weakness. Today, confess it to the Lord and pray for that person. If you are ready, also pray one sentence of blessing for someone who has hurt you.
lessons.quick: The Lord prayed for Peter before he fell; I too will pray first, then speak.
text: The Lord said, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat,
but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.”
He said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death!”
He said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will by no means crow today until you deny that you know me three times.”

lessons.title: Watching Over All People and Our City
lessons.hear:
This week we began with praying for one another; we saw Epaphras striving in prayer, Paul’s longing for intercession, and the Lord Jesus praying for Peter.
