Today the scope of our intercession widens further: “I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks, be made for all men: for kings and all who are in high places” (1 Timothy 2:1-2).

Paul says this comes “first of all.” The church prays not only for itself but also for its city, its nation, and those in authority. Why? Because God “desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). Intercession is the prelude to the gospel; the church’s prayers prepare people’s hearts.

When the Israelites were taken captive to Babylon, God told them through Jeremiah: “Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace” (Jeremiah 29:7). Whether you live in Taipei, Kuala Lumpur, Singapore, Auckland, or any other city, that city is the place where God has stationed you to keep watch.

Multiplication means letting intercession become the culture of the church, not just the burden of a few. You can invite a brother or sister to become your prayer partner and exchange prayer requests at a set time each week. You can lead a time of prayer for the city in your small group, praying for schools, hospitals, the government, and workplaces. You can also teach your children to pray for a friend before bed.

God once said, “I sought for a man among them who would build up the wall, and stand in the gap before me for the land” (Ezekiel 22:30). May God find among us not just one person, but a whole company keeping watch together.
lessons.light: One purpose: to build God’s system. The Lord’s Prayer says, “Your Kingdom come,” and intercession is asking for God’s kingdom to come in my city. From one person keeping watch to a whole company keeping watch, from my small group to my city—this is change from the inside out: first life, then relationships, then ministry.
think: In 1 Timothy 2:1-4, whom does Paul want us to pray for? Why?
What new insight or change have I experienced in intercession this week?
Whom will I invite to join me in keeping regular watch over our fellow members and our city?
lessons.speak: Father, you desire all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth. Make our church a church that keeps watch over its city—praying for those in authority, for the city where I live, and for friends and family who don’t yet believe. Give me a prayer partner, too, so that together we can stand in the gap and see your kingdom come in this land. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a brother or sister to become your prayer partner and agree on a set time each week to exchange prayer requests. The first time you meet, spend five minutes praying together for the city where you live.
lessons.quick: Stand in the gap and keep watch—for fellow members, for pastors, and for my city.
text: I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men,
for kings and all who are in high places, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence.
For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior,
who desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth.

weeks.title: Small Groups: The Basic Unit of Body Life
weeks.keyText: Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
weeks.theme: No one should follow Jesus alone; the small group is the family where we know one another, shepherd one another, and grow up together.
group: Read Acts 2:44-47. What did the early church do “at home”? Which of these draws you the most?
Have you ever been truly caught and held by a small group (in person or online)—or have you ever wanted to leave one? Share how that felt.
What can our small group do this week for someone who has been absent or is new? Who will do it, and when?
weeks.sunday: Sunday is the big gathering; the small group is the little family—and we need both. This Lord’s Day, look for the members of your group in the congregation, sit a little closer, and share a meal together afterward. During the service, pray quietly for your small group leader. When you get home, post one sentence in your group chat about what you received from the message, so that Sunday’s word keeps rising like yeast in your little household.

lessons.title: In the Temple and at Home
lessons.hear:
On the day of Pentecost, three thousand people were baptized. Overnight, Jerusalem had a huge crowd of brand-new believers, and the apostles faced a very practical question: how do you shepherd this many people? Luke records their answer: “Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart” (Acts 2:46).

Notice the two locations: “in the temple” and “at home.” The temple was the large gathering, where everyone worshiped together and listened to the apostles’ teaching. The home was the small gathering, where a few families sat around one table to eat, pray, and share their lives. The early church did not choose one over the other; it walked on two legs. With only the large gathering, people easily become spectators. With only the small gathering, people easily turn inward. The large gathering lets us see how vast God’s family is; the small gathering lets us be known and remembered.

There is real warmth in the picture of “breaking bread at home.” Around a dinner table, it is hard to keep a mask on for long. Who has lost their appetite today, whose child just got sick, who has been unusually quiet lately—none of it stays hidden in a small circle. That is exactly the value of a small group: it is the basic unit of body life. Just as the human body is made up of countless cells, and the body is healthy only when each cell is healthy, so it is with the church. A church’s health is often seen not from the pulpit but in living rooms, around dinner tables, and even in the little squares on a video-call screen.

The result is plain to see: “The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved” (Acts 2:47). God entrusts new life to a warm community. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes: you are not only a member of a church, but also part of a small “church at home.”
lessons.light: A self-centered person joins a small group asking, “What can this group give me?” A selfless person asks, “Lord, You have placed me among these few people—how do You want me to love them?” Life first, then relationships, then ministry: the small group is the very first place where life flows into relationships. Here, “let Jesus reign” is not a slogan; it means letting Him be the host at the table and in our sharing.
think: In Acts 2:44-47, what did the believers do in the temple, and what did they do at home?
Does my faith life lean more toward “the temple” or more toward “the home”?
How can I invest more in my small group this week—or start looking for one?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank You that You do not leave me to follow You alone, but have placed me in Your household. Forgive me for often treating my small group as an optional program, preferring to sit quietly in the big service. Help me, like the early church, to share the table with my brothers and sisters with gladness and singleness of heart, so that our small group becomes a home where You are the host. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, leave a message in your group chat or send a private note to your small group leader: “Thank you for this group—I want to be more involved.” If you don’t yet have a small group, ask a ministry team member today how to join one.
lessons.quick: Worship together in the temple, know one another at home—a church walking on both legs is a healthy church.
text: All who believed were together, and had all things in common.
They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.
Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.

lessons.title: No One Should Believe Alone
lessons.hear:
One brother had been a Christian for eight years. He never missed a Sunday, yet he always politely declined to join a small group. His reasons sounded perfectly sensible: “I’m busy with work, I’m an introvert, and my faith is between me and God.” For years his life looked steady. Then his company laid people off. He was out of work for six months, began losing sleep, and grew colder and colder toward God’s Word. He still sat in the back row every Sunday, but no one noticed that he was slowly sinking—because no one really knew him.

“My faith is between me and God” is only half true. Salvation is indeed personal; no one can believe on your behalf. But growth in faith happens in community. The writer of Hebrews urges us to “exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called ‘today’, lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). A hard heart does not happen overnight; it hardens bit by bit in isolation. The remedy is not a once-a-year conference but “exhort one another day by day”—and that takes a group of people who truly know you.

Ecclesiastes saw this long ago: “For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:10). At creation, God saw that everything was good—except for one thing: “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18). Those words speak first about marriage, yet they also reveal God’s purpose in making us: human beings are made for relationship.

Eventually a coworker brought that brother into a small workplace group. The first time he shared, he got only one sentence out before his voice broke. Six months later he said, “I used to think small groups were for weak people. Then I discovered that I was the weak one—and God had long since prepared hands to lift me up.”
lessons.light: “I don’t need a small group” is often not strength but the self-protection of a self-centered life: afraid of being seen, afraid of being asked for something, afraid of the hassle. The old mindset says faith is a private matter; God’s view says faith is personal, but never solitary. When I move from the human perspective to God’s perspective, I begin to see my small group as God’s hand lifting me up—and as my hand for lifting up others.
think: According to Hebrews 3:12-14, how does a heart become hardened step by step?
Do I carry the thought, “My faith is between me and God”? What am I afraid of underneath it?
Which one or two members of the body am I willing to let know me more truly?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often want to handle my struggles on my own. I tell myself that not bothering anyone is maturity, when really I am afraid of letting my weakness be seen. Tear down the walls in my heart. Make me willing to be known and to be supported, and willing to reach out my hand to lift up brothers and sisters who have fallen. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in your small group or with one member of the body you trust, share one real need you have right now and ask them to pray for you. You don’t have to say it all perfectly—just say the first sentence.
lessons.quick: Salvation is personal, but growth is communal; no one should follow Jesus alone.
text: Beware, brothers, lest perhaps there might be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, in falling away from the living God;
but exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called “today”, lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
For we have become partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence firm to the end,

lessons.title: Open Your Door
lessons.hear:
Readers often skip the last chapter of Romans, because it is a long list of greetings and names. But read it slowly and you will find a treasure: “Greet the assembly that is in their house” (Romans 16:5). Prisca and Aquila were a tentmaking couple. They were not apostles or elders, yet they turned their home into a place where the church gathered. In Corinth they took in Paul; in Ephesus they mentored Apollos; in Rome they opened their door again. Wherever they went, their home became a church.

Today’s practice is to learn from their example. Opening your door doesn’t require a big living room or great cooking—just a heart willing to let others come in. It can be a simple dinner with a few people at your place, a regular corner table at a coffee shop, or an online video room. Many small groups in the Kingdom 321 Air Fellowship are family members in different countries and time zones “breaking bread” together through a screen. The form differs, but the essence is the same: “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them” (Matthew 18:20).

A healthy small group has three simple marks:
1. People are remembered—someone checks in when they’re absent, and someone celebrates their birthday;
2. People are heard—when they share, no one rushes to give answers; we listen to the end first;
3. People are held up—when there is a need, everyone actually steps in to help.

You don’t need to wait until you become a small group leader to start doing these three things. Any member can be the one who makes the group feel more like home. Prisca and Aquila had no titles, yet all the churches of the Gentiles gave thanks for them. What God values is not your position, but the door you open to the members of His body.
lessons.light: The practice of 920 happens right here in the small group: every member is one of my “2,” the people God has placed beside me; I practice the selfless “0” so that the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit, the “9,” can grow in our relationships. People matter more than programs—a small group’s format can be simple, but its attention to people must never be skipped. A small group is not a program; it is a family who belong to one another.
think: In Romans 16:3-5, how does Paul describe Prisca and Aquila?
Who in my small group may not have been remembered, heard, or held up lately?
What “door” can I open for that person today?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank You for turning ordinary homes into places of Your presence. Use my home, my time, and my screen so that brothers and sisters can be remembered, heard, and held up here. May the door of my home be open to You and to the members of Your body. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose one small group member and care for them in the way they most need: check in if they’ve been absent, help if they have a need, or invite them this week to your home or online for a cup of tea and a fifteen-minute chat.
lessons.quick: No title required—just open the door, and a home can become a church.
text: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus,
who risked their own necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the assemblies of the Gentiles.
Greet the assembly that is in their house. Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the first fruits of Achaia to Christ.

lessons.title: The Night Thomas Was Missing
lessons.hear:
On the night the risen Lord first appeared to His disciples, Thomas wasn’t there. Scripture doesn’t say where he went; it only says he “wasn’t with them when Jesus came” (John 20:24). Perhaps he was discouraged; perhaps he didn’t want to face a group of men who had failed just as he had. The result: everyone else saw the Lord, while he only heard about it—and his heart filled with even more doubt.

Thomas’s restoration happened in the very same place: “After eight days again his disciples were inside and Thomas was with them” (John 20:26). The Lord appeared to him when the community was gathered. When Thomas came back among the brothers, he met the Lord and spoke the highest confession in John’s entire Gospel: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28).

Today, take an honest look at how you show up in your small group. Self-centeredness has more than one face. Some are often absent and always have a reason. Some are present in body but not in heart—camera off during the online meeting, scrolling through another window. Some turn sharing time into their own stage. Some only listen and never speak, always keeping a safe distance. And some carry what they hear in the group and repeat it elsewhere. All of these weaken the most basic cell in the body.

Online small groups are God’s grace for this generation, letting people scattered far and wide be one in heart. Paul himself wrote, “For though I am absent in the flesh, yet I am with you in the spirit” (Colossians 2:5). The key is not the screen but whether your heart is present. The adjustments can be very concrete: log on on time, turn on your camera, close other windows, and truly listen when it’s someone else’s turn. When possible, find chances to meet group members in person.

One gentle word as well: if you have been hurt in a small group, stepping back for a while is nothing to be ashamed of. But ask the Lord to keep you from staying outside forever. Like Thomas, come back with your honest questions; the Lord is often waiting for you among your brothers and sisters.
lessons.light: In a small group, the self-centered person either wants to be the star or only wants to be an audience; the selfless person is a member of the body—present, engaged, trustworthy with confidences, and listening. Humility is returning to my proper place: not grabbing the spotlight, and not hiding either. The focus is on Jesus—not on my own performance, and not on other people’s flaws. When I return to my proper place, my small group gains one more real member.
think: In John 20:24-29, what resulted from Thomas’s absence, and what resulted from his return?
Which form of self-centeredness shows up most often in me in my small group?
At the next small group meeting, which specific habit will I adjust?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that in my small group I am sometimes absent, sometimes distracted, and sometimes only want to talk about myself. Thank You that You did not give up on Thomas, and You have not given up on me. Help me to be present in body and in heart, and to meet You again among my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down one habit you will adjust at your next small group (for example: being on time, turning on your camera, speaking less and listening more, keeping confidences). Tell your small group leader or a group member and ask them to remind you.
lessons.quick: Thomas met the Lord when he came back to the brothers; I too will be present in body and in heart.
text: But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, wasn’t with them when Jesus came.

The other disciples therefore said to him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”
After eight days, again his disciples were inside and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, the doors being locked, and stood in the middle, and said, “Peace be to you.”
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

lessons.title: One Home Gives Birth to Another
lessons.hear:
When Paul said farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus, he looked back on three years of ministry: “I didn’t shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, teaching you publicly and from house to house” (Acts 20:20). Once again, two locations—the public gathering and one home after another. This great apostle did not just stand behind a pulpit; he walked through door after door, making disciples household by household.

This week we have seen that the small group is the basic unit of body life: the early church met in the temple and at home; no one should follow Jesus alone; an ordinary home can become a church; and we need to be present in heart as well as in body. Now we take one more step: healthy life always multiplies. Cells divide, and one home gives birth to another.

Moses’ father-in-law Jethro once gave him wise advice: choose God-fearing men from among the people and “place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens” (Exodus 18:21), so that the burden would be shared by many. The smallest unit was “ten,” so that everyone had someone looking after them. Today’s small groups work the same way: it is not one pastor caring for hundreds of people alone, but in every small group some are being shepherded and others are beginning to learn how to shepherd.

Multiplication doesn’t have to mean launching a new group right away. It can start with something small: inviting a new friend to your group, walking alongside a new member through their first three months, or letting your small group leader know, “I’m willing to learn to lead.” The best fruit of a healthy small group, a few years down the road, is not a meeting that gets more and more crowded, but new shepherds who have grown up from within it.
lessons.light: The last step in the eight steps of changing a mindset is multiplication. The practice of 235 begins in the small group: here you find spiritual companions (2); here someone becomes your spiritual parent, and you in turn become a spiritual parent to others (3). To let Jesus receive all the glory does not mean my small group gets bigger; it means His kingdom expands.
think: In Acts 20:18-21, in what two settings did Paul teach the believers?
How has my view of small groups changed this week?
Whom can I invite to my small group, or which new member can I walk alongside?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You for placing me in a small household. Make this household healthy, and make it fruitful so that it gives birth to new households. Give me courage to invite new friends, patience to walk with new members, and prepare me to learn to lead when You call me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, pray for a friend or newcomer who doesn’t yet have a small group, and sometime this week invite them to a small group meeting (in person or online), or have one conversation with them.
lessons.quick: A healthy small group multiplies: some are shepherded, and some are learning to shepherd.
text: When they had come to him, he said to them, “You yourselves know, from the first day that I set foot in Asia, how I was with you all the time,
serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears, and with trials which happened to me by the plots of the Jews;
how I didn’t shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, teaching you publicly and from house to house,
testifying both to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God and faith toward our Lord Jesus.
